options.rationale: Transcribe produces a transcript but cannot determine intent or manage a conversation.

options.text: Amazon Kendra

options.text: Amazon Lex

Transcribe would only produce a transcript, and the other services address search and fraud scoring.

options.text: Amazon Fraud Detector
options.rationale: Fraud Detector scores risk for events such as transactions, not call routing.

options.rationale: Amazon SageMaker AI is the platform for building, training, tuning, and deploying custom models, including tabular algorithms such as gradient boosting, with control over code and hyperparameters. Amazon Bedrock provides API access to managed foundation models with customization limited to techniques such as fine-tuning and continued pre-training on those models, not arbitrary algorithms.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock, because custom tabular models must be accessed through foundation model APIs
options.rationale: Tabular models are not served through foundation model APIs.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker AI, because it is the only service that can host an inference endpoint
options.rationale: Bedrock also serves inference, so exclusivity of hosting is not the reason.

questions.question: A city transit authority is reviewing two candidate projects: (A) issuing fare refunds according to a published refund policy table, and (B) predicting which stations will exceed platform capacity next month. Which two statements correctly assess these projects? (Select TWO.)

questions.question: A hospital network wants to reduce patient appointment no-shows and has asked a data science team to build a model. Which activity should the team complete FIRST in the ML development lifecycle?

options.text: Split the historical appointment data into training, validation, and test sets.
options.rationale: Data splitting happens after the business goal is set and data has been collected and explored.

options.text: Select a classification algorithm and run a training job in Amazon SageMaker AI.
options.rationale: Algorithm selection and training come later; choosing a model before framing the problem risks solving the wrong task.

options.text: Define the business goal and the success metrics that the model must improve.
options.rationale: The ML lifecycle starts with identifying the business goal and framing the ML problem, including the measurable business metrics that define success. Without an agreed goal and metric, the team cannot judge whether any model is worth deploying. Data collection, training, and deployment all follow from that framing.

options.text: Deploy a real-time inference endpoint so clinicians can begin testing predictions.
options.rationale: Deployment is one of the last stages and only makes sense after a model has been trained and evaluated.

questions.question: A logistics company has raw delivery data in Amazon S3 that needs cleaning, joining, and transformation before training. The team wants a visual, low-code way to explore and prepare the data inside Amazon SageMaker AI with minimal custom code. Which capability should the team use?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
options.rationale: SageMaker Data Wrangler provides a visual interface for data exploration, cleaning, transformation, and feature preparation, and it can export the resulting flow as a repeatable processing job. It targets the data preparation stage of the lifecycle without requiring the team to hand-write transformation pipelines.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
options.rationale: Model Monitor watches deployed models for drift and quality issues; it does not prepare training data.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
options.rationale: Model Registry catalogs and versions trained models; it has no data transformation features.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning
options.rationale: Automatic Model Tuning searches hyperparameter values during training, not data preparation.

questions.question: A financial services company finds that features computed for model training differ slightly from the features computed at inference time, causing inconsistent predictions. The company wants a central, versioned store so the same feature definitions serve both training and real-time inference. Which SageMaker AI capability meets this requirement?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
options.rationale: Ground Truth builds labeled datasets; it does not serve features at inference time.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Experiments
options.rationale: Experiments tracks training runs and their metrics, not reusable feature data.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Canvas
options.rationale: Canvas is a no-code environment for building models, not a feature repository.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
options.rationale: SageMaker Feature Store is a purpose-built repository for storing, sharing, and versioning features, with an offline store for training and an online store for low-latency inference. Serving both paths from the same definitions is what eliminates training-serving skew.

questions.question: A manufacturing company has 80,000 unlabeled images of parts and needs high-quality defect labels before it can train a supervised computer vision model. Which AWS service should the company use to create the labeled training dataset?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Autopilot
options.rationale: Autopilot trains and tunes candidate models automatically but requires labeled data as input.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
options.rationale: SageMaker Ground Truth manages data labeling workflows, letting a company use human workforces and automated labeling to produce annotated training datasets. Labeling belongs to the data collection and preparation stage that precedes training.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
options.rationale: Pipelines orchestrates lifecycle steps; it does not annotate raw data.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
options.rationale: Clarify analyzes bias and explains predictions; it does not create labels.

questions.question: A gaming company is preparing a tabular dataset of player sessions for churn modeling. Which two activities are part of data preprocessing and feature engineering? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Imputing missing values in the session duration column.
options.rationale: Preprocessing and feature engineering transform raw records into model-ready inputs: handling missing data, scaling numeric columns, encoding categorical variables, and deriving new features. Endpoint sizing, registry approvals, and operational alarms all belong to later deployment and monitoring stages.

options.text: Choosing the number of inference instances for the production endpoint.
options.rationale: Instance sizing is a deployment decision made after a model is trained.

options.text: Publishing the approved model version to a model registry.
options.rationale: Registering an approved model happens after evaluation, not during data preparation.

options.text: Encoding the categorical device type column into numeric values.
options.rationale: Preprocessing and feature engineering transform raw records into model-ready inputs: handling missing data, scaling numeric columns, encoding categorical variables, and deriving new features. Endpoint sizing, registry approvals, and operational alarms all belong to later deployment and monitoring stages.

options.text: Configuring an alarm on endpoint invocation errors.
options.rationale: Endpoint error alarms are part of production monitoring.

questions.question: A media streaming company trains a binary classifier that predicts whether a viewer will cancel a subscription. Only 3 percent of viewers cancel, and the model reports 97 percent accuracy while catching almost no cancellations. Which metric should the team use to measure how many actual cancellations the model detects?

options.text: Recall
options.rationale: Recall (sensitivity) is the fraction of actual positives that the model correctly identifies, so it directly exposes missed cancellations. With a heavily imbalanced dataset, overall accuracy is misleading because predicting the majority class always looks good.

options.text: Precision
options.rationale: Precision measures how many predicted cancellations were real, not how many real cancellations were found.

options.text: Mean squared error
options.rationale: Mean squared error evaluates regression models with continuous targets, not classification.

options.text: R-squared
options.rationale: R-squared describes variance explained in regression problems, not classification coverage.

questions.question: A public sector agency built a model that forecasts monthly water consumption in liters. Which two metrics are appropriate for evaluating this regression model? (Select TWO.)

options.text: F1 score
options.rationale: F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall for classification tasks.

options.text: Root mean squared error
options.rationale: Regression models predict continuous values, so error-based metrics apply: RMSE squares errors before averaging and therefore penalizes large misses more heavily, while MAE averages absolute errors and treats all deviations proportionally. F1, AUC-ROC, and accuracy are classification metrics that require discrete class labels.

options.text: Area under the ROC curve
options.rationale: AUC-ROC summarizes ranking quality of a classifier, not regression error.

options.text: Mean absolute error
options.rationale: Regression models predict continuous values, so error-based metrics apply: RMSE squares errors before averaging and therefore penalizes large misses more heavily, while MAE averages absolute errors and treats all deviations proportionally. F1, AUC-ROC, and accuracy are classification metrics that require discrete class labels.

options.text: Accuracy
options.rationale: Accuracy is a classification metric and is undefined for continuous targets.

questions.question: A retail company is starting its first ML project. Place the ML development lifecycle stages in the correct order.

options.rationale: The lifecycle runs from business framing to data work, then model training and tuning, then evaluation and deployment, and finally ongoing monitoring and retraining. The loop is iterative: monitoring findings feed new data collection and training cycles rather than ending the project.

options.text: 1. Monitor the deployed model and retrain when performance degrades. → 2. Evaluate the model and deploy it to an inference endpoint. → 3. Train and tune a candidate model. → 4. Collect, explore, and prepare the data. → 5. Identify the business goal and frame the ML problem.
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Collect, explore, and prepare the data. → 2. Train and tune a candidate model. → 3. Evaluate the model and deploy it to an inference endpoint. → 4. Monitor the deployed model and retrain when performance degrades. → 5. Identify the business goal and frame the ML problem.
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

questions.question: A logistics company must run inference on a 400 GB file of shipment records once each night and does not need real-time responses. The company wants to avoid paying for idle infrastructure between runs. Which Amazon SageMaker AI inference option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: A real-time endpoint with automatic scaling
options.rationale: A real-time endpoint bills for running instances continuously and is designed for low-latency single requests.

options.text: A batch transform job
options.rationale: Batch transform starts compute resources, processes a whole dataset from Amazon S3, writes results back, then shuts the resources down, so nothing runs between nightly jobs. Real-time and always-warm endpoints bill for provisioned capacity even when no requests arrive.

options.text: An asynchronous inference endpoint kept warm at one instance
options.rationale: Asynchronous inference suits large individual payloads with long processing times, and holding one warm instance still costs money.

options.text: A multi-model real-time endpoint
options.rationale: A multi-model endpoint reduces cost when hosting many models, but it is still a persistent real-time endpoint.

questions.question: A healthcare startup has an internal application with unpredictable, intermittent traffic and long idle periods. The team wants a low-latency inference option that scales to zero automatically and requires no instance management. Which Amazon SageMaker AI deployment option should the team choose?

options.text: Batch transform
options.rationale: Batch transform processes datasets offline and cannot answer application requests synchronously.

options.text: Real-time inference on a provisioned instance
options.rationale: Provisioned real-time instances stay billed during long idle periods and require sizing decisions.

options.text: Asynchronous inference
options.rationale: Asynchronous inference queues requests for long-running, large payloads rather than returning immediate responses.

options.text: Serverless inference
options.rationale: SageMaker serverless inference provisions and scales compute automatically based on request volume and scales to zero when idle, so the team pays only for what it uses without choosing instance types. It fits spiky, intermittent workloads that still need synchronous responses.

questions.question: A finance company deployed a credit risk model six months ago and notices that predictions have become less reliable as economic conditions change. Which two statements correctly describe drift? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Data drift is a training-time problem in which the model memorizes noise in the training set.
options.rationale: Memorizing training noise describes overfitting, which is a training-time issue, not drift.

options.text: Data drift occurs when the statistical distribution of production input data differs from the training data.
options.rationale: Data drift is a shift in the distribution of production inputs relative to training data, while concept drift is a change in the underlying relationship between inputs and the target. Both degrade deployed model quality over time, are detected through production monitoring, and typically trigger retraining.

options.text: Drift affects only deep learning models, not tree-based models.
options.rationale: Drift is a property of data and real-world relationships, so it affects any model type.

options.text: Drift is detected during hyperparameter tuning before the model is deployed.
options.rationale: Drift emerges in production after deployment; tuning happens before deployment.

options.text: Concept drift occurs when the relationship between the input features and the target variable changes.
options.rationale: Data drift is a shift in the distribution of production inputs relative to training data, while concept drift is a change in the underlying relationship between inputs and the target. Both degrade deployed model quality over time, are detected through production monitoring, and typically trigger retraining.

questions.question: A retail company wants automatic detection of data quality issues and statistical deviations in the inputs and predictions of a production Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, with alerts when metrics breach a baseline. Which capability should the company use?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Experiments
options.rationale: Experiments organizes and compares training runs; it does not observe live endpoints.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
options.rationale: Feature Store stores and serves features; it does not raise drift alerts.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
options.rationale: SageMaker Model Monitor captures endpoint data, compares it against a baseline computed from training data, and reports violations for data quality, model quality, bias drift, and feature attribution drift. It is the monitoring building block of the lifecycle.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
options.rationale: Data Wrangler prepares data before training and has no production monitoring role.

questions.question: An insurance company must prove to auditors which dataset version, preprocessing code, training container, and hyperparameters produced each production model version. Which MLOps practice does this requirement describe?

options.text: Hyperparameter optimization
options.rationale: Hyperparameter optimization searches for the best training parameters; it does not record provenance.

options.text: Prompt engineering
options.rationale: Prompt engineering shapes inputs to generative models and is unrelated to audit trails.

options.text: Data augmentation
options.rationale: Data augmentation expands training data with transformed copies; it does not document artifact history.

options.text: Lineage tracking
options.rationale: Lineage tracking records the chain of artifacts and steps, including data versions, code, containers, parameters, and resulting models, so any deployed model can be traced back to exactly what produced it. This supports auditability, repeatability, and troubleshooting across the lifecycle.

questions.question: A business analyst at a retail company with no coding experience wants to build a demand forecasting model using a visual, no-code interface. Which Amazon SageMaker AI capability should the analyst use?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Canvas
options.rationale: SageMaker Canvas provides a no-code visual interface where business analysts can import data, build models, and generate predictions without writing code. Training Jobs, Pipelines, and the Model Registry are developer-oriented capabilities that assume ML engineering skills.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Training Jobs
options.rationale: Training Jobs run containerized training code and require ML engineering work.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
options.rationale: Model Registry versions and approves trained models; it does not build them.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
options.rationale: Pipelines defines CI/CD-style workflows in code, which is not a no-code experience.

questions.question: A media company's data scientists run dozens of training runs per week with different algorithms and parameters. They struggle to remember which run produced which metrics. Which Amazon SageMaker AI capability lets them automatically track, organize, and compare training runs?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
options.rationale: Ground Truth is for labeling data, not tracking training runs.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Experiments
options.rationale: SageMaker Experiments (available as MLflow-based experiment tracking in SageMaker AI) captures parameters, metrics, and artifacts for each training run so teams can compare runs side by side and reproduce results. Experiment tracking is the MLOps practice that makes model development repeatable.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
options.rationale: Clarify detects bias and explains predictions; it does not organize experiments.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Serverless Inference
options.rationale: Serverless inference is a deployment option, not an experimentation tool.

questions.question: A manufacturing company wants to adopt MLOps practices for its quality inspection models. Which two practices are core MLOps principles? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Versioning datasets, code, and models so results can be reproduced.
options.rationale: MLOps applies DevOps discipline to ML: version everything (data, code, models) for repeatability, and automate build, test, and deployment through CI/CD so releases are reliable and frequent. Monitoring in production is also essential, and centralized governed storage beats local copies.

options.text: Increasing the model's temperature parameter to improve creativity.
options.rationale: Temperature is a generative AI inference setting, not an MLOps practice.

options.text: Automating the build, test, and deployment of models through CI/CD pipelines.
options.rationale: MLOps applies DevOps discipline to ML: version everything (data, code, models) for repeatability, and automate build, test, and deployment through CI/CD so releases are reliable and frequent. Monitoring in production is also essential, and centralized governed storage beats local copies.

options.text: Storing all training data exclusively on local laptops for speed.
options.rationale: Local, unmanaged data copies undermine reproducibility and governance.

options.text: Disabling monitoring after deployment to reduce operational cost.
options.rationale: Removing monitoring hides drift and quality regressions, the opposite of MLOps.

questions.question: A gaming company trains a fraud detection model and wants to find the best combination of learning rate and tree depth by launching many training jobs automatically and comparing their validation scores. Which Amazon SageMaker AI capability performs this search?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
options.rationale: JumpStart provides pretrained models and solution templates, not hyperparameter search.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
options.rationale: Model Monitor tracks deployed model quality, not training-time parameters.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
options.rationale: Data Wrangler prepares data and does not run training jobs.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning
options.rationale: Automatic Model Tuning (hyperparameter tuning) launches multiple training jobs with different hyperparameter values, using strategies such as Bayesian optimization to converge on the combination that maximizes the chosen objective metric. It automates the tuning stage of the lifecycle.

questions.question: A bank's fraud team says that flagging a legitimate transaction as fraud costs far more in customer goodwill than missing an occasional fraudulent one. When evaluating candidate models, which metric should the team prioritize?

options.text: Precision
options.rationale: Precision is the fraction of positive predictions that are actually positive, so maximizing it minimizes false positives, which here are legitimate transactions wrongly flagged. Recall would instead prioritize catching every fraud at the cost of more false alarms, the opposite of this business preference.

options.text: Recall
options.rationale: Recall reduces missed frauds (false negatives), which the team said is the cheaper error.

options.text: Mean absolute error
options.rationale: Mean absolute error applies to regression outputs, not a fraud classification decision.

options.text: Training loss
options.rationale: Training loss measures fit on training data and does not reflect business error costs.

questions.question: A public health team wants a single table showing how many of its disease-screening predictions were true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. Which evaluation artifact provides this view?

options.text: An ROC curve
options.rationale: An ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate across thresholds; it does not list raw counts.

options.text: A confusion matrix
options.rationale: A confusion matrix tabulates predicted versus actual classes, exposing the four outcome counts from which accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 are derived. It is the standard starting point for diagnosing which kind of error a classifier makes.

options.text: A learning curve
options.rationale: A learning curve shows performance as training data or epochs increase.

options.text: A feature importance chart
options.rationale: Feature importance ranks input influence and says nothing about error types.

questions.question: A retail company wants to compare two classifiers across all possible decision thresholds to see which one separates buyers from non-buyers better overall. Which metric summarizes this threshold-independent ranking quality?

options.text: Accuracy at a 0.5 threshold
options.rationale: Accuracy at a single fixed threshold ignores behavior at other operating points and is misleading with imbalance.

options.text: Root mean squared error
options.rationale: RMSE evaluates continuous predictions, not class separation.

options.text: Area under the ROC curve
options.rationale: AUC-ROC aggregates classifier performance over all thresholds into one value between 0 and 1, where 0.5 is random guessing and 1.0 is perfect separation. Because it does not fix a threshold, it is useful for comparing models before the operating point is chosen.

options.text: Number of training epochs
options.rationale: Epoch count is a training setting, not a performance measure.

questions.question: An ML team's model reaches 99 percent accuracy on training data but only 68 percent on the held-out test set. Which two actions are appropriate responses to this pattern? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Train for many more epochs on the same training data.
options.rationale: More epochs on the same data typically worsens overfitting rather than improving generalization.

options.text: Apply regularization or reduce model complexity.
options.rationale: A large gap between strong training performance and weak test performance indicates overfitting: the model memorized noise instead of learning generalizable patterns. Standard remedies are regularization, simpler models, early stopping, and collecting more diverse training data. Training longer on the same data usually deepens the overfit.

options.text: Remove the test set and evaluate only on training data.
options.rationale: Discarding held-out evaluation hides the problem instead of fixing it.

options.text: Increase the amount and diversity of training data.
options.rationale: A large gap between strong training performance and weak test performance indicates overfitting: the model memorized noise instead of learning generalizable patterns. Standard remedies are regularization, simpler models, early stopping, and collecting more diverse training data. Training longer on the same data usually deepens the overfit.

options.text: Raise the inference endpoint instance size.
options.rationale: Instance size affects latency and throughput, not generalization.

questions.question: A logistics company wants to automate its end-to-end ML workflow so that data processing, training, evaluation, conditional model approval, and deployment run as one repeatable, versioned workflow triggered by new data. Which Amazon SageMaker AI capability should the company use?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Canvas
options.rationale: Canvas is a no-code model building tool, not a workflow orchestrator.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
options.rationale: Feature Store stores features; it does not run multi-step workflows.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards
options.rationale: Model Cards document model details for governance; they do not execute steps.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
options.rationale: SageMaker Pipelines is a purpose-built CI/CD orchestration service for ML that defines steps such as processing, training, evaluation, conditional logic, model registration, and deployment as a repeatable directed workflow. Each execution is tracked, which supports repeatability and lineage.

questions.question: A healthcare company needs a governed place to store trained model versions, attach approval status, and let a deployment pipeline pick up only approved versions. Which Amazon SageMaker AI capability meets this requirement?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Studio
options.rationale: Studio is the integrated development environment for ML work, not a versioned model catalog.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
options.rationale: SageMaker Model Registry catalogs models in versioned model package groups, records metadata, and tracks approval status so automated deployment steps can promote only approved versions. It is the governance handoff between training and deployment.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
options.rationale: Ground Truth handles data labeling.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning
options.rationale: Automatic Model Tuning searches hyperparameters during training.

questions.question: A data science team at an energy company wants a single integrated development environment where members can write notebooks, run training jobs, deploy models, and view experiment results. Which Amazon SageMaker AI capability provides this?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Batch Transform
options.rationale: Batch transform is an offline inference option, not a development environment.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
options.rationale: Clarify computes bias and explainability reports.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Studio
options.rationale: SageMaker Studio is the unified web-based IDE for ML, bringing notebooks, data preparation, training, tuning, deployment, and monitoring views into one interface. The other options are individual capabilities used within or alongside Studio.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
options.rationale: Model Monitor watches production endpoints for drift.

questions.question: A retail company wants to accelerate a product image classification project by starting from an existing pretrained model and an example solution template instead of training from scratch. Which Amazon SageMaker AI capability should the team use?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
options.rationale: Data Wrangler prepares data; it does not supply pretrained models.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Experiments
options.rationale: Experiments tracks runs rather than providing model artifacts.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
options.rationale: SageMaker JumpStart offers a catalog of pretrained models, including foundation models, plus deployable solution templates and example notebooks that can be fine-tuned on a company's own data. It shortens time to market compared with building and training a model from zero.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
options.rationale: Feature Store manages feature data, not models.

questions.question: A lending company must explain which input features most influenced individual loan decisions and check whether the training data underrepresents certain groups. Which Amazon SageMaker AI capability addresses both needs?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
options.rationale: SageMaker Clarify computes pre-training and post-training bias metrics and produces feature attribution explanations for individual and overall predictions. Model Monitor can then track bias and attribution drift in production using Clarify-generated baselines.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
options.rationale: Model Registry versions models and records approval status; it computes no bias metrics.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
options.rationale: Pipelines orchestrates steps but does not itself analyze bias or explainability.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Canvas
options.rationale: Canvas builds models without code and is not a bias analysis service.

questions.question: A telecom company wants to document each production model's intended use, training data description, evaluation results, and known limitations in a single governance artifact for internal review. Which Amazon SageMaker AI feature should the company use?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
options.rationale: Model Monitor detects drift in production data and predictions.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
options.rationale: Ground Truth builds labeled datasets.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning
options.rationale: Automatic Model Tuning optimizes hyperparameters.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards
options.rationale: SageMaker Model Cards create a single record of a model's purpose, training details, evaluation metrics, risk rating, and limitations to support governance and audits. AWS AI Service Cards serve a similar documentation purpose but for AWS managed AI services, not customer models.

questions.question: An e-commerce company is deciding how to measure the success of a new recommendation model beyond technical accuracy. Which two are business metrics rather than model performance metrics? (Select TWO.)

options.text: F1 score on the validation set
options.rationale: F1 is a statistical classification metric computed on labeled data.

options.text: Return on investment from increased order value
options.rationale: Business metrics measure organizational outcomes such as ROI, cost per user, conversion rate, customer feedback, and time to market. Model metrics such as F1, AUC, and RMSE measure statistical quality and can improve without moving any business outcome, which is why both categories are tracked.

options.text: Area under the ROC curve
options.rationale: AUC-ROC is a model ranking quality metric.

options.text: Average customer satisfaction score after launch
options.rationale: Business metrics measure organizational outcomes such as ROI, cost per user, conversion rate, customer feedback, and time to market. Model metrics such as F1, AUC, and RMSE measure statistical quality and can improve without moving any business outcome, which is why both categories are tracked.

options.text: Root mean squared error on held-out data
options.rationale: RMSE quantifies prediction error, not business value.

questions.question: A ride-hailing company observes that its arrival-time model's accuracy has declined even though incoming data distributions look unchanged; rider behavior itself has changed since a new city transit line opened. Which condition best describes this situation?

options.text: Concept drift
options.rationale: Concept drift is a change in the underlying relationship between the input features and the target, so the learned mapping becomes stale even when input distributions look similar. Retraining on recent data that reflects the new behavior is the standard remedy.

options.text: Overfitting to the validation set
options.rationale: Validation overfitting would appear before deployment, not as a gradual post-launch decline tied to real-world change.

options.text: Insufficient endpoint capacity
options.rationale: Capacity limits cause latency or throttling, not systematically wrong predictions.

options.text: Feature store latency
options.rationale: Feature retrieval latency affects response time, not predictive relationships.

questions.question: A logistics company wants to retrain its route-optimization model automatically whenever monitoring detects that prediction quality has fallen below an agreed threshold. Which approach implements this with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Have an engineer manually rerun the notebook each quarter.
options.rationale: Manual quarterly reruns add ongoing human effort and miss degradation between runs.

options.text: Use Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor alerts to trigger an Amazon SageMaker Pipelines execution that retrains and registers the model.
options.rationale: A retraining trigger connects monitoring signals to an automated pipeline: Model Monitor detects a quality or drift violation, emits an alert, and that event starts a SageMaker Pipelines run that reprocesses data, retrains, evaluates, and registers a new version. Manual reruns and fixed calendars react late and cost more effort.

options.text: Increase the size of the inference instance so predictions improve.
options.rationale: Larger instances change throughput and latency, not predictive quality.

options.text: Turn off monitoring and rebuild the model annually from scratch.
options.rationale: Removing monitoring eliminates the very signal needed to know when retraining is required.

questions.question: A data science team is preparing data for a supervised churn model. Place these data-focused activities in the order they occur in the ML lifecycle.

options.text: 1. Split the prepared dataset into training, validation, and test sets. → 2. Engineer new features such as tenure buckets and usage ratios. → 3. Clean the data by removing duplicates and imputing missing values. → 4. Perform exploratory data analysis to understand distributions and missing values. → 5. Collect raw records from source systems into Amazon S3.
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Perform exploratory data analysis to understand distributions and missing values. → 2. Clean the data by removing duplicates and imputing missing values. → 3. Engineer new features such as tenure buckets and usage ratios. → 4. Split the prepared dataset into training, validation, and test sets. → 5. Collect raw records from source systems into Amazon S3.
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Perform exploratory data analysis to understand distributions and missing values. → 2. Collect raw records from source systems into Amazon S3. → 3. Clean the data by removing duplicates and imputing missing values. → 4. Engineer new features such as tenure buckets and usage ratios. → 5. Split the prepared dataset into training, validation, and test sets.
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Collect raw records from source systems into Amazon S3. → 2. Perform exploratory data analysis to understand distributions and missing values. → 3. Clean the data by removing duplicates and imputing missing values. → 4. Engineer new features such as tenure buckets and usage ratios. → 5. Split the prepared dataset into training, validation, and test sets.
options.rationale: Data work flows from collection, to exploratory analysis that reveals quality issues and patterns, to cleaning and preprocessing, to feature engineering that creates model-ready inputs, and finally to splitting the dataset so training, validation, and testing use separate data. Splitting last (or before any statistics that could leak) preserves honest evaluation.

questions.question: A data science team at an agriculture company has collected a new crop yield dataset and is beginning exploratory data analysis. Which two activities belong to this stage? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploying the model to a serverless endpoint for testing.
options.rationale: Deployment publishes a trained model for inference and does not profile raw data.

options.text: Setting the learning rate for the training job.
options.rationale: Learning rate selection belongs to training and hyperparameter tuning.

options.text: Calculating summary statistics to understand feature distributions and outliers.
options.rationale: Exploratory data analysis happens after data collection and before preprocessing; the team profiles the data with summary statistics and visualizations to find quality problems, outliers, imbalances, and relationships that shape feature engineering and modeling choices.

options.text: Configuring data capture on a production endpoint.
options.rationale: Data capture supports production monitoring, which occurs after deployment.

options.text: Creating visualizations to examine correlations between variables.
options.rationale: Exploratory data analysis happens after data collection and before preprocessing; the team profiles the data with summary statistics and visualizations to find quality problems, outliers, imbalances, and relationships that shape feature engineering and modeling choices.

questions.question: A genomics startup runs inference on individual payloads up to 800 MB, and each request takes about 20 minutes of processing. Requests arrive sporadically throughout the day and callers can poll for results. Which Amazon SageMaker AI inference option fits these requirements?

options.text: Serverless inference
options.rationale: Serverless inference has small payload and short timeout limits unsuited to 800 MB, 20-minute jobs.

options.text: Asynchronous inference
options.rationale: SageMaker asynchronous inference queues incoming requests, handles payloads up to about 1 GB with long processing times, delivers results to Amazon S3, and can scale the instance count to zero when the queue is empty. Real-time and serverless options enforce much smaller payload and timeout limits.

options.text: Real-time inference
options.rationale: Real-time endpoints are built for low-latency responses and cap payload size and request duration well below these needs.

options.text: Batch transform on an hourly schedule
options.rationale: Hourly batch runs add up to an hour of avoidable waiting for sporadic single requests.

questions.question: A retail company completed offline evaluation of a new demand forecast model and wants confidence before fully replacing the current production model. Which two deployment practices reduce release risk? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Shift a small percentage of live traffic to the new model and compare results before full cutover.
options.rationale: Canary or blue/green style traffic shifting exposes the new model to a small real workload with a quick rollback path, and shadow testing compares the challenger against the production model on live traffic without customer impact. Deleting the old version or releasing to everyone at once removes the safety net.

options.text: Delete the previous model version immediately after deploying the new one.
options.rationale: Keeping the prior version enables fast rollback if the new model misbehaves.

options.text: Use shadow testing to send production traffic copies to the new model without affecting responses.
options.rationale: Canary or blue/green style traffic shifting exposes the new model to a small real workload with a quick rollback path, and shadow testing compares the challenger against the production model on live traffic without customer impact. Deleting the old version or releasing to everyone at once removes the safety net.

options.text: Skip evaluation on the test set because validation metrics were strong.
options.rationale: The held-out test set guards against overfitting to validation choices.

options.text: Deploy directly to all users at once to shorten time to market.
options.rationale: A big-bang release maximizes blast radius if the model has issues.

questions.question: A startup wants to shorten time to market for a text classification feature. The team uploads a labeled CSV and wants Amazon SageMaker AI to automatically explore algorithms, preprocess data, train candidate models, and rank them by quality with little manual work. Which capability does this?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Autopilot
options.rationale: SageMaker Autopilot (AutoML) automatically preprocesses data, selects algorithms, trains and tunes multiple candidates, and presents a ranked leaderboard with full visibility into generated notebooks. It compresses several lifecycle stages into an automated flow, reducing time to market.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards
options.rationale: Model Cards document models for governance rather than training them.

Placing evaluation before registration and registration before deployment enforces governance in CI/CD for ML.

Run a processing step that validates and transforms the new data.

Register the model version in the Model Registry pending approval. → 4. Deploy the approved model version to the production endpoint. → 5. Run a processing step that validates and transforms the new data.
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

Evaluate the trained model against the held-out test data and check the quality threshold. → 4. Register the model version in the Model Registry pending approval. → 5. Deploy the approved model version to the production endpoint.
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

questions.question: A logistics company wants to use one large pre-trained model as the starting point for several different applications, including shipment summaries, a customer chatbot, and translated notifications. Which term describes a model that is pre-trained on broad data and can be adapted to many downstream tasks?

options.text: A classification model
options.rationale: A classification model predicts a label for one specific task and is not broadly adaptable.

options.text: A forecasting model
options.rationale: A forecasting model predicts future numeric values from time series data only.

options.text: A clustering model
options.rationale: A clustering model groups unlabeled records and does not generate text.

options.text: A foundation model
options.rationale: A foundation model (FM) is a large model pre-trained on a very large, broad dataset that can then be adapted to many different tasks through prompting, retrieval augmentation, or fine-tuning. That general-purpose reuse is what separates an FM from a traditional model built for one narrow prediction task.

questions.question: A media company is reviewing how a large language model processes the text it receives. Before the model can process a sentence, the text is split into smaller units such as words or word fragments. What are these units called?

options.text: Features
options.rationale: Features are input variables in traditional machine learning, not text units for an LLM.

options.text: Labels
options.rationale: Labels are the target values used in supervised training, not pieces of input text.

options.text: Tokens
options.rationale: Tokenization breaks input text into tokens, which are the units a large language model actually reads and generates. A token is often a whole short word or a fragment of a longer word, which is why token counts do not match word counts exactly.

options.text: Epochs
options.rationale: An epoch is one full pass over a training dataset during training.

questions.question: A healthcare provider sends a 400-page policy manual to a foundation model in a single prompt and receives an error stating that the input is too long. Which model characteristic explains this limit?

options.text: The context window, which caps the number of tokens the model can process at once
options.rationale: The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can handle in a single request, counting both the prompt and the generated completion. Long documents must be chunked, summarized in stages, or retrieved selectively so that only relevant portions enter the context window.

options.text: The embedding dimension, which caps the length of each input document
options.rationale: Embedding dimension describes the size of a vector representation, not the input limit for a prompt.

options.text: The temperature setting, which caps how much text the model reads
options.rationale: Temperature affects randomness in the output and has no effect on input length.

options.text: The number of model parameters, which caps the size of an input file
options.rationale: Parameter count relates to model capacity, not to the per-request token limit.

questions.question: A public sector agency wants to find documents that discuss the same idea as a user question even when the documents use different wording. Which representation of text supports this capability?

options.text: A keyword inverted index built from exact terms
options.rationale: A keyword index matches literal terms and misses paraphrases that use different words.

options.text: A one-hot encoding of every unique word in the corpus
options.rationale: One-hot encoding treats every word as unrelated, so it captures no semantic similarity.

options.text: A compressed archive of the raw document files
options.rationale: Compressing files changes storage size and provides no way to compare meaning.

options.text: An embedding, which is a numeric vector that captures semantic meaning
options.rationale: An embedding maps text to a vector of numbers so that passages with similar meaning sit close together in vector space. Similarity search over embeddings therefore matches on meaning rather than on exact shared words, which is the basis of semantic search and retrieval augmented generation.

questions.question: A gaming company is building a semantic search feature and needs to store embeddings and run similarity queries against them. Which AWS options can serve as a vector store for this workload? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service
options.rationale: Amazon OpenSearch Service supports vector fields and k-nearest-neighbor search, and Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL supports vector columns and similarity operators through the pgvector extension. Both can hold embeddings alongside metadata and answer nearest-neighbor queries for semantic search or retrieval augmented generation.

options.text: Amazon Athena
options.rationale: Athena runs SQL queries over data in Amazon S3 and is not a vector index.

options.text: AWS Glue Data Catalog
options.rationale: The Glue Data Catalog stores table metadata and does not store or search vectors.

options.text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension
options.rationale: Amazon OpenSearch Service supports vector fields and k-nearest-neighbor search, and Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL supports vector columns and similarity operators through the pgvector extension. Both can hold embeddings alongside metadata and answer nearest-neighbor queries for semantic search or retrieval augmented generation.

options.text: Amazon QuickSight
options.rationale: QuickSight is a business intelligence and dashboarding service, not a vector store.

questions.question: A finance team asks a foundation model to draft a quarterly earnings summary. The instruction and supporting text the team sends to the model is called the prompt. What is the model-generated text that comes back called?

options.text: The completion
options.rationale: In generative AI, the input to the model is the prompt and the generated output is the completion, also called the response or inference result. Both prompt and completion consume tokens, which is why they are billed and limited together.

options.text: The checkpoint
options.rationale: A checkpoint is a saved snapshot of model weights during training.

options.text: The gradient
options.rationale: A gradient is a value used to update weights while training, not model output.

options.text: The hyperparameter
options.rationale: A hyperparameter is a training or inference setting chosen by a person.

questions.question: A manufacturing company uses a foundation model to write internal safety bulletins and needs the wording to be consistent and predictable for the same prompt. Which inference parameter change BEST supports this requirement?

options.text: Increase the temperature value
options.rationale: Raising temperature increases randomness, producing more variation between runs.

options.text: Lower the temperature value toward 0
options.rationale: Temperature controls randomness during token selection. A low temperature makes the model strongly favor the highest-probability tokens, producing focused and repeatable output, while a high temperature flattens the distribution and yields more varied and creative text.

options.text: Increase the maximum token count
options.rationale: Maximum token count limits response length and does not affect word choice randomness.

options.text: Add more stop sequences
options.rationale: Stop sequences end generation at a marker; they do not make wording more consistent.

questions.question: A retail company wants the model to consider only the smallest set of candidate tokens whose cumulative probability reaches a chosen threshold at each generation step. Which inference parameter provides this behavior?

options.text: Top-k
options.rationale: Top-k limits sampling to a fixed number of candidate tokens, not a cumulative probability.

options.text: Max tokens
options.rationale: Max tokens caps the length of the response and does not filter candidates.

options.text: Top-p
options.rationale: Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest group of highest-probability tokens whose probabilities add up to the value of p, so the candidate pool grows or shrinks with the model's confidence. Top-k instead keeps a fixed count of candidates regardless of how the probability mass is distributed.

options.text: Stop sequences
options.rationale: Stop sequences terminate generation when specific text appears.

questions.question: A telecom support tool must stop generating text as soon as the model produces the string "###END###" so the response can be parsed reliably. Which inference parameter should the team configure?

options.text: Top-k
options.rationale: Top-k controls how many candidate tokens are considered at each step.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Temperature controls randomness, not where generation ends.

options.text: Stop sequences
options.rationale: A stop sequence is a string that tells the model to end generation immediately when it is produced, which keeps responses within a predictable structure. Length caps such as max tokens cut output at an arbitrary point instead of at a meaningful boundary.

options.text: Top-p
options.rationale: Top-p controls the cumulative probability threshold for candidate tokens.

questions.question: An insurance company notices that a foundation model produced a confident answer citing a regulation that does not exist. What is this behavior called?

options.text: Overfitting
options.rationale: Overfitting describes a trained model that memorizes training data and generalizes poorly.

options.text: Data drift
options.rationale: Data drift is a change in production data distribution over time.

options.text: Class imbalance
options.rationale: Class imbalance is an uneven distribution of labels in a training dataset.

options.text: Hallucination
options.rationale: A hallucination is output that is fluent and confident but factually wrong or fabricated, because the model predicts likely text rather than looking up verified facts. Grounding the model with retrieved source documents and adding human review reduces the impact of hallucinations.

questions.question: A legal services firm includes three labeled example question-and-answer pairs inside the prompt so the model matches the firm's expected answer style. Which prompting technique is this?

options.text: Zero-shot prompting
options.rationale: Zero-shot prompting includes an instruction with no worked examples.

options.text: Continued pre-training
options.rationale: Continued pre-training updates model weights with large amounts of unlabeled domain data.

options.text: Few-shot prompting
options.rationale: Few-shot prompting places a small number of input and output examples in the prompt so the model can infer the desired pattern at inference time. Zero-shot prompting gives only the instruction with no examples, and neither approach changes the model weights.

options.text: Reinforcement learning from human feedback
options.rationale: RLHF is a training process that aligns a model using human preference data.

questions.question: A research group needs a model that accepts both a photograph and a text question in the same request and returns a written answer about the image. Which type of model meets this requirement?

options.text: A unimodal text-only model
options.rationale: A unimodal text model can process only text input and cannot interpret an image.

options.text: A multimodal model
options.rationale: A multimodal model accepts or produces more than one data modality, such as text plus images, audio, or video. A unimodal model handles a single modality only, so it cannot interpret an image alongside a text question.

options.text: A tabular regression model
options.rationale: A tabular regression model predicts numeric values from structured columns.

options.text: A text embedding model
options.rationale: An embedding model returns vectors for similarity search, not written answers.

questions.question: An advertising agency wants to generate original product images from written descriptions. Which class of generative model is designed for this image generation task?

options.text: Diffusion models
options.rationale: Diffusion models learn to reverse a gradual noising process, so they can start from random noise and progressively denoise it into an image that matches a text prompt. They are the dominant architecture behind current text-to-image generation.

options.text: Decision tree ensembles
options.rationale: Tree ensembles handle structured prediction tasks and cannot synthesize images.

options.text: Linear regression models
options.rationale: Linear regression predicts a numeric value from input features.

options.text: K-means clustering models
options.rationale: K-means groups similar records and generates no new content.

questions.question: An engineering team is explaining why modern large language models handle long passages better than earlier recurrent networks. Which component of the transformer architecture is the key reason?

options.text: Convolution layers that scan local pixel neighborhoods
options.rationale: Convolutions capture local spatial patterns and are typical of vision networks.

options.text: Recurrent cells that pass a hidden state one step at a time
options.rationale: Recurrent cells are the earlier approach that transformers replaced.

options.text: The self-attention mechanism that weighs relationships among all tokens in the sequence
options.rationale: Transformers use self-attention so that every token can be compared against every other token in the input at once, which captures long-range dependencies and allows highly parallel training. Recurrent architectures process tokens sequentially, which makes long dependencies harder to learn.

options.text: Pooling layers that reduce the size of feature maps
options.rationale: Pooling downsamples feature maps in convolutional networks.

questions.question: A hospital is preparing a large collection of clinical guideline PDFs for retrieval augmented generation. Why does the team split each document into smaller passages before creating embeddings?

options.text: Chunking keeps each passage within embedding input limits and improves retrieval precision
options.rationale: Chunking divides long documents into passages that fit the embedding model's input limit and that each cover a focused topic. Smaller, coherent chunks return more relevant matches and waste less of the generation model's context window than whole documents would.

options.text: Chunking removes the need to store any vectors
options.rationale: Chunks still must be embedded and stored in a vector store to be searchable.

options.text: Chunking increases the number of parameters in the foundation model
options.rationale: Chunking is a data preparation step and does not change model size.

options.text: Chunking converts the PDFs into structured relational tables
options.rationale: Chunking splits text into passages; it does not produce relational schemas.

questions.question: Place the stages of the foundation model lifecycle in the correct order, from the earliest stage to the latest.

options.text: 1. Select and prepare the training data → 2. Pre-train the model on the broad dataset → 3. Fine-tune the model on task-specific labeled data → 4. Evaluate the model against benchmarks and business metrics → 5. Deploy the model and collect feedback for continuous improvement
options.rationale: The foundation model lifecycle begins with data selection and preparation, followed by pre-training on the broad corpus. Adaptation such as fine-tuning comes next, then evaluation against benchmarks and business metrics, and finally deployment with ongoing feedback that drives later iterations.

options.text: 1. Deploy the model and collect feedback for continuous improvement → 2. Evaluate the model against benchmarks and business metrics → 3. Fine-tune the model on task-specific labeled data → 4. Pre-train the model on the broad dataset → 5. Select and prepare the training data
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Pre-train the model on the broad dataset → 2. Fine-tune the model on task-specific labeled data → 3. Evaluate the model against benchmarks and business metrics → 4. Deploy the model and collect feedback for continuous improvement → 5. Select and prepare the training data
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Pre-train the model on the broad dataset → 2. Select and prepare the training data → 3. Fine-tune the model on task-specific labeled data → 4. Evaluate the model against benchmarks and business metrics → 5. Deploy the model and collect feedback for continuous improvement
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

questions.question: A university help desk receives thousands of repetitive questions about enrollment deadlines and wants an application that holds a natural back-and-forth conversation with students. Which generative AI use case does this describe?

options.text: Anomaly detection
options.rationale: Anomaly detection flags unusual records and does not converse with users.

options.text: Time series forecasting
options.rationale: Forecasting predicts future numeric values from historical series.

options.text: A conversational chatbot
options.rationale: A conversational chatbot uses a foundation model to interpret free-form questions and respond in natural language while keeping earlier turns of the conversation in context. The other options are traditional machine learning tasks that do not involve generating dialogue.

options.text: Image segmentation
options.rationale: Image segmentation labels regions of an image at the pixel level.

questions.question: A software company wants its developers to receive inline suggestions for functions and unit tests directly in the IDE, based on natural language comments. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this use case?

options.text: Amazon Q Developer
options.rationale: Amazon Q Developer is the generative AI assistant for software development, offering in-IDE code suggestions, code explanation, test generation, and troubleshooting help. Amazon Q Business targets enterprise knowledge questions over company content rather than writing code in an IDE.

options.text: Amazon Q Business
options.rationale: Amazon Q Business answers questions over enterprise data; it is not an IDE coding assistant.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend
options.rationale: Comprehend performs natural language processing tasks such as entity and sentiment extraction.

options.text: Amazon Kendra
options.rationale: Kendra provides intelligent enterprise search over documents.

questions.question: A news publisher is cataloging generative AI use cases it can pursue with foundation models. Which two tasks are well suited to a text-generating foundation model? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Condensing long investigative articles into short abstracts
options.rationale: Summarization and creative text generation are core foundation model use cases because both require producing fluent new language from a given input. Fraud detection, revenue forecasting, and video compression are handled by traditional machine learning or by non-AI engineering techniques.

options.text: Detecting fraudulent credit card transactions in real time
options.rationale: Fraud detection is a supervised classification or anomaly detection problem.

options.text: Drafting alternative headlines for an article in several tones
options.rationale: Summarization and creative text generation are core foundation model use cases because both require producing fluent new language from a given input. Fraud detection, revenue forecasting, and video compression are handled by traditional machine learning or by non-AI engineering techniques.

options.text: Forecasting next quarter's subscription revenue
options.rationale: Revenue forecasting uses time series models on historical numeric data.

options.text: Compressing video files to reduce storage cost
options.rationale: Video compression is a codec engineering task, not generative AI.

questions.question: A travel company wants a generative AI application that can decide which internal APIs to call, chain the calls together, and complete a multi-step booking change on behalf of a customer. Which Amazon Bedrock capability is designed for this?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
options.rationale: Guardrails apply content filters and topic restrictions; they do not orchestrate API calls.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Agents use a foundation model to break a request into steps, invoke configured APIs or functions, and iterate until the task is complete. Knowledge Bases supply retrieved context, Guardrails filter content, and Model Evaluation compares model quality, so none of those orchestrate actions.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation
options.rationale: Model Evaluation compares model performance and does not execute business actions.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
options.rationale: Knowledge Bases retrieve relevant documents to ground responses, not to call APIs.

questions.question: A gaming studio already runs its player profile data in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and wants to add semantic search over player support tickets without introducing a new database engine. Which approach involves the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Migrate all data to Amazon Neptune Analytics and store vectors as graph properties
options.rationale: A migration to a graph service is a large change when the existing database already supports vectors.

options.text: Enable the pgvector extension in the existing Aurora PostgreSQL cluster and store embeddings there
options.rationale: The pgvector extension adds a vector data type and similarity operators to Aurora PostgreSQL, so embeddings can live beside existing relational data with no new engine to run. Introducing a separate database or a hand-built search service adds infrastructure and operational work for the same result.

options.text: Build a custom nearest-neighbor service on Amazon EC2 instances
options.rationale: Self-managing a nearest-neighbor service on EC2 maximizes operational overhead.

options.text: Store embeddings as CSV files in Amazon S3 and scan them with AWS Lambda for each query
options.rationale: Scanning CSV files per query does not scale and provides no vector index.

questions.question: A logistics company stores hundreds of millions of embeddings that are queried a few times per hour for batch enrichment jobs, and cost is the primary concern rather than millisecond latency. Which AWS option is MOST cost-effective for this vector workload?

options.text: Amazon MemoryDB with vector search
options.rationale: MemoryDB keeps vectors in memory for single-digit millisecond search, which is costly at this scale.

options.text: Amazon S3 Vectors
options.rationale: Amazon S3 Vectors provides durable vector storage with built-in similarity query support at S3-scale economics, which suits very large vector sets queried infrequently. In-memory and provisioned cluster options deliver much lower latency but cost far more when queries are rare.

options.text: Amazon DocumentDB with vector search
options.rationale: DocumentDB vector search runs on provisioned instances that stay billed between infrequent queries.

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service provisioned clusters sized for peak load
options.rationale: Provisioning OpenSearch clusters for peak load wastes capacity for a few queries per hour.

questions.question: A financial services firm needs sub-millisecond vector similarity lookups to personalize offers while a customer is still in the mobile app session. Which AWS service is designed for in-memory vector search at this latency?

options.text: Amazon MemoryDB
options.rationale: Amazon MemoryDB is an in-memory database with durability that supports vector search, making it a fit when the application requires the lowest possible retrieval latency. Disk-based relational, analytics, or graph options are appropriate for vectors but are not tuned for in-memory response times.

options.text: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
options.rationale: RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector is disk-based and cannot match in-memory latency.

options.text: Amazon Redshift
options.rationale: Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics queries, not a low-latency vector lookup store.

options.text: Amazon Neptune Analytics
options.rationale: Neptune Analytics analyzes graph data with vector support but is not an in-memory cache.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical research team wants to combine graph relationships between compounds with vector similarity over research abstracts in a single analytics engine. Which AWS service supports graph analytics with built-in vector search?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB
options.rationale: DynamoDB is a key-value and document store without native vector similarity search.

options.text: Amazon Neptune Analytics
options.rationale: Amazon Neptune Analytics is a graph analytics engine that supports vector similarity search alongside graph traversals, so relationship analysis and semantic similarity can run together. DocumentDB also supports vectors but stores JSON documents rather than graph relationships.

options.text: Amazon DocumentDB
options.rationale: DocumentDB supports vector search over JSON documents but is not a graph analytics engine.

options.text: Amazon Timestream
options.rationale: Timestream is purpose-built for time series data.

questions.question: A global retailer needs product reviews written in Japanese converted into English for its analytics team, with high accuracy and minimal setup. Which AWS service should the company use?

options.text: Amazon Transcribe
options.rationale: Transcribe converts recorded speech into text; it does not translate written reviews.

options.text: Amazon Textract
options.rationale: Textract pulls text and structure out of scanned documents and forms.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend
options.rationale: Comprehend analyzes text for sentiment, entities, and topics without translating it.

options.text: Amazon Translate
options.rationale: Amazon Translate is the managed neural machine translation service for converting text between languages. Transcribe converts speech to text, Textract extracts text from documents, and Comprehend analyzes text for entities and sentiment rather than translating it.

questions.question: A customer support platform sets the max tokens inference parameter too low for a summarization request. What is the MOST likely result?

options.text: The response is cut off before the summary is complete
options.rationale: Max tokens caps how many tokens the model may generate in the response, so a value that is too low truncates the output mid-thought. It is a hard length limit, not a quality control, and it does not change which model runs.

options.text: The model refuses to answer the prompt
options.rationale: A low output cap truncates text; it does not cause a refusal.

options.text: The response becomes more factually accurate
options.rationale: Response length limits have no direct effect on factual accuracy.

options.text: The model switches to a smaller foundation model automatically
options.rationale: Inference parameters never swap the underlying model.

questions.question: A marketing team wants a brainstorming assistant that produces highly varied and surprising campaign slogans across repeated runs of the same prompt. Which combination of inference settings BEST fits this goal?

options.text: Low temperature with a very small top-k value
options.rationale: Low temperature and small top-k restrict choices, producing repetitive output.

options.text: Temperature of 0 with greedy decoding
options.rationale: Temperature 0 selects the most likely token every time, minimizing variety.

options.text: Higher temperature with a larger top-p value
options.rationale: Raising temperature flattens the token probability distribution and raising top-p widens the candidate pool, so together they increase diversity and creativity in the output. Deterministic settings such as temperature 0 produce nearly identical responses on every run.

options.text: A short max tokens limit with extra stop sequences
options.rationale: Length caps and stop sequences shape response length, not creativity.

questions.question: A bank is documenting the risks of using a public foundation model chatbot for customer-facing answers about loan products. Which two limitations of foundation models should the documentation highlight? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The model can generate plausible but incorrect statements
options.rationale: Foundation models can hallucinate confident but wrong content, and their parametric knowledge stops at the training cutoff, so answers about newer rates or policies require grounding through retrieval or fine-tuning. Models do not inherently cite verified sources, refuse out-of-scope topics, or retrain themselves during use.

options.text: The model always refuses questions about topics outside its training data
options.rationale: Models typically attempt an answer even outside their training data, which drives hallucination risk.

options.text: The model's knowledge is frozen at a training cutoff unless it is grounded with current data
options.rationale: Foundation models can hallucinate confident but wrong content, and their parametric knowledge stops at the training cutoff, so answers about newer rates or policies require grounding through retrieval or fine-tuning. Models do not inherently cite verified sources, refuse out-of-scope topics, or retrain themselves during use.

options.text: The model automatically cites verified sources for every claim it makes
options.rationale: Base models generate text without verified citations unless a retrieval system supplies sources.

options.text: The model retrains itself on each customer conversation by default
options.rationale: Inference does not update model weights; conversations do not retrain the model by default.

questions.question: A streaming media service wants to suggest movies to each viewer based on that viewer's watch history and the behavior of similar users. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this recommendation use case?

options.text: Amazon Rekognition
options.rationale: Rekognition analyzes images and video for objects, faces, and moderation.

options.text: Amazon Polly
options.rationale: Polly converts text into lifelike speech.

options.text: Amazon Lex
options.rationale: Lex builds conversational voice and text bots.

options.text: Amazon Personalize
options.rationale: Amazon Personalize is the managed recommendation service that trains on user interaction data to produce personalized item rankings. Recommendations are listed as an AI use case alongside generative tasks, but they use specialized recommender models rather than a chatbot or vision service.

questions.question: A nonprofit is building a retrieval augmented generation pipeline to make its grant archive searchable by meaning. Place the ingestion steps in the correct order.

options.text: 1. Store the embeddings in a vector database → 2. Generate an embedding for each chunk with an embedding model → 3. Split the documents into appropriately sized chunks → 4. Collect and clean the source documents
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Split the documents into appropriately sized chunks → 2. Generate an embedding for each chunk with an embedding model → 3. Store the embeddings in a vector database → 4. Collect and clean the source documents
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Collect and clean the source documents → 2. Split the documents into appropriately sized chunks → 3. Generate an embedding for each chunk with an embedding model → 4. Store the embeddings in a vector database
options.rationale: RAG ingestion starts by collecting and cleaning the source content, then chunking it into passages sized for the embedding model. Each chunk is converted into an embedding vector, and the vectors are stored in a vector database where similarity search can retrieve them at query time.

options.text: 1. Split the documents into appropriately sized chunks → 2. Collect and clean the source documents → 3. Generate an embedding for each chunk with an embedding model → 4. Store the embeddings in a vector database
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

questions.question: A city government asks a foundation model to classify citizen emails into five categories using only a written instruction that describes each category, with no examples included. Which prompting technique is being used?

options.text: Zero-shot prompting
options.rationale: Zero-shot prompting relies entirely on the model's pre-trained knowledge and the instruction itself, with no demonstrations in the prompt. Adding one example makes it one-shot, and several examples make it few-shot; none of these change the model's weights.

options.text: Few-shot prompting
options.rationale: Few-shot prompting would include labeled example emails in the prompt.

options.text: Fine-tuning
options.rationale: Fine-tuning trains the model on labeled data and updates its weights.

options.text: Retrieval augmented generation
options.rationale: RAG retrieves external documents to ground responses, which this scenario does not do.

questions.question: A company compares two ways to make a foundation model answer with its private product terminology: adding retrieved product documents to each prompt, or fine-tuning the model on labeled product Q&A pairs. Which statement correctly contrasts the two approaches?

options.text: Fine-tuning keeps documents current automatically, while retrieval requires retraining for every update
options.rationale: This reverses the two approaches; retrieval is the one that stays current without retraining.

options.text: Retrieval grounds answers in up-to-date documents without changing model weights, while fine-tuning bakes knowledge and style into the weights
options.rationale: Retrieval augmented generation injects current documents into the prompt at inference time, so content updates require only re-indexing, not retraining. Fine-tuning changes the model weights, which is better for teaching style or task behavior but must be repeated when knowledge changes.

options.text: Both approaches modify the model weights but retrieval does so at lower cost
options.rationale: Retrieval does not modify weights at all; only fine-tuning does.

options.text: Retrieval can only be used with image models, while fine-tuning works for text
options.rationale: Retrieval augmented generation is used widely with text models.

questions.question: Which statement BEST describes a large language model (LLM)?

options.text: A rules engine that matches keywords to canned responses
options.rationale: Rules engines follow hand-written patterns and cannot generalize like an LLM.

options.text: A database that stores sentences for exact retrieval
options.rationale: LLMs generate new text token by token rather than retrieving stored sentences.

options.text: A speech synthesis system that converts text to audio
