questions.question: A financial services company must choose between two foundation models for a summarization feature. The team wants automatic metric scoring on its own prompt dataset plus an option to collect human reviewer ratings, all within a managed AWS workflow. Which capability should the team use?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
options.rationale: Prompt Management stores, versions, and tests prompts but does not run scored model comparisons.

options.text: SageMaker Feature Store
options.rationale: Feature Store manages ML features for traditional model training and serving.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
options.rationale: Guardrails enforce safety policies at inference time and produce no comparative quality scores.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation
options.rationale: Bedrock Model Evaluation supports automatic evaluation with built-in metrics and datasets, LLM-as-a-judge scoring, and human evaluation workflows using your own workforce. It is the managed way to compare candidate models on your data before committing. Results guide model selection rather than enforcing runtime policy.

questions.question: A media archive holds thousands of scanned contracts, product images, recorded interviews, and video clips. The company wants a managed way to extract structured insights from all of these formats to feed a generative AI application. Which capability is purpose-built for this?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Data Automation
options.rationale: Bedrock Data Automation transforms unstructured multimodal content such as documents, images, audio, and video into structured output that applications and knowledge bases can consume. It removes the need to stitch together separate extraction pipelines per media type. That structured output is often used to populate a knowledge base for RAG.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
options.rationale: Prompt Management organizes prompts, not multimodal content extraction.

options.text: SageMaker Ground Truth
options.rationale: Ground Truth coordinates human data labeling for training datasets.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
options.rationale: Provisioned Throughput is a capacity commitment option unrelated to content extraction.

questions.question: A platform team maintains dozens of prompt templates for a customer-support assistant on Amazon Bedrock. They need to version the templates, test variations, and let applications reference a prompt by identifier instead of hardcoding text. Which Amazon Bedrock capability meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
options.rationale: Prompt Management is a Bedrock capability for creating, versioning, comparing, and sharing prompts, which applications and Flows can then reference by identifier. Centralizing prompts avoids scattering template text through application code and makes iteration auditable. It manages the prompts themselves, not documents or model weights.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
options.rationale: Knowledge Bases index documents for retrieval, not prompt templates.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock playgrounds
options.rationale: Playgrounds allow ad hoc experimentation but provide no versioned prompt library referenced by applications.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation
options.rationale: Model Distillation produces smaller student models and has nothing to do with prompt storage.

questions.question: A data science team wants to use a specialized third-party foundation model that is not among Amazon Bedrock's directly integrated serverless models. They want to discover, subscribe to, and deploy it while still calling it through Bedrock APIs. Which option enables this?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Marketplace
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Marketplace gives access to a broad catalog of specialized and emerging foundation models beyond the directly integrated serverless set; you deploy a chosen model to managed endpoints and invoke it through Bedrock APIs. It extends model choice while keeping a consistent development experience. Note that Marketplace models typically run on dedicated endpoints rather than fully serverless capacity.

options.text: SageMaker Model Cards
options.rationale: SageMaker Model Cards document a model's details for governance; they are not a model catalog for deployment.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
options.rationale: Guardrails enforce content policies, not model discovery.

options.text: AWS AI Service Cards
options.rationale: AWS AI Service Cards are transparency documents about AWS AI services, not a marketplace.

questions.question: An enterprise wants an out-of-the-box generative AI assistant that employees can ask questions about internal HR policies, wikis, and SharePoint content, with answers restricted to documents each employee is authorized to see. The company wants to avoid building a RAG application. Which AWS service should it choose?

options.text: Amazon Q Developer
options.rationale: Amazon Q Developer assists with software development tasks such as coding and AWS guidance.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock playgrounds
options.rationale: Playgrounds test prompts against models and have no enterprise data connectors or permission awareness.

options.text: PartyRock
options.rationale: PartyRock is a public playground for learning to build small AI apps, not a permission-aware enterprise assistant.

options.text: Amazon Q Business
options.rationale: Amazon Q Business is a ready-made generative AI assistant that connects to enterprise data sources through built-in connectors and respects existing document permissions when answering employee questions. It delivers the RAG experience as a product, so no application development is required. Building the equivalent yourself on Bedrock would be the higher-effort alternative.

questions.question: A software team wants inline code suggestions in the IDE, help scanning code for security issues, and a chat assistant that can explain AWS resources and errors. Which AWS service meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon Q Business
options.rationale: Amazon Q Business answers questions over company data for general employees, not IDE code assistance.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
options.rationale: JumpStart provides pretrained models and solution templates inside SageMaker AI, not IDE completions.

options.text: Amazon Q Developer
options.rationale: Amazon Q Developer is the generative AI assistant for software development: it provides code completion in IDEs, code transformation, security scanning, and conversational help with AWS services in the console and CLI. Amazon Q Business targets general enterprise knowledge work rather than coding. Choosing between the two Q products by audience is a commonly tested distinction.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents
options.rationale: Bedrock Agents are building blocks for custom applications, not an off-the-shelf developer assistant.

questions.question: Business analysts at a retail chain want to type natural language questions such as 'Why did sales dip in March?' and receive charts and narrative summaries inside their existing AWS business intelligence dashboards. Which capability should they use?

options.text: Amazon Q in QuickSight
options.rationale: Amazon Q in QuickSight adds generative BI to Amazon QuickSight, letting users ask data questions in natural language, generate visuals, build data stories, and get executive summaries of dashboards. It embeds generative AI where the analytics already live. Amazon Q in Connect serves contact-center agents, a different persona entirely.

options.text: Amazon Q in Connect
options.rationale: Amazon Q in Connect gives real-time suggested responses and actions to contact center agents.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
options.rationale: Knowledge Bases ground custom applications in documents; they do not generate BI dashboards.

options.text: SageMaker Canvas
options.rationale: SageMaker Canvas is a no-code interface for building ML models, not conversational dashboard analytics.

questions.question: A telecom's contact center agents struggle to find answers during live calls. The company wants generative AI to detect caller intent in real time and surface recommended responses and knowledge articles to agents inside their contact center workspace. Which AWS capability meets this requirement?

options.text: Amazon Q Developer
options.rationale: Amazon Q Developer supports software development workflows, not live call assistance.

options.text: Amazon Q in Connect
options.rationale: Amazon Q in Connect is the generative AI capability of Amazon Connect that analyzes live conversations, infers intent, and delivers recommended responses and relevant knowledge content to agents in real time. It is embedded in the contact center rather than being a general assistant. This persona fit is the key discriminator among the Amazon Q offerings.

options.text: PartyRock
options.rationale: PartyRock is a learning playground for building simple AI apps, unsuitable for production contact centers.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation
options.rationale: Model Evaluation compares foundation model quality offline.

questions.question: A university instructor wants students with no AWS account experience to build small generative AI demo apps in a browser to learn prompt engineering. Which AWS offering is intended for this kind of hands-on learning?

options.text: SageMaker Studio
options.rationale: SageMaker Studio is a full ML IDE that requires AWS account setup and ML knowledge.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
options.rationale: Provisioned Throughput is a production capacity purchase, not a learning environment.

options.text: PartyRock
options.rationale: PartyRock is a shareable, browser-based playground where anyone can build small generative AI apps and experiment with prompts without writing code or configuring AWS infrastructure. It is a learning and exploration tool rather than a production platform. Production applications belong on Amazon Bedrock.

options.text: Amazon Q Business
options.rationale: Amazon Q Business is an enterprise assistant that requires connecting company data sources.

questions.question: An ML team wants to browse pretrained open-source and proprietary models, review example notebooks, and deploy or fine-tune a chosen model inside a SageMaker AI environment where they control instance types. Which capability should they use?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock playgrounds
options.rationale: Bedrock playgrounds test prompts against managed models and expose no instance choices or notebooks.

options.text: SageMaker Model Monitor
options.rationale: Model Monitor watches deployed endpoints for drift; it is not a model hub.

options.text: Amazon Q Developer
options.rationale: Amazon Q Developer assists with coding tasks rather than hosting model catalogs.

options.text: SageMaker JumpStart
options.rationale: SageMaker JumpStart is a model and solution hub inside SageMaker AI that offers pretrained models, example notebooks, and one-click deployment or fine-tuning onto instances you select. It suits teams that want more control over the training and hosting stack than Bedrock's serverless model access provides. Bedrock is the choice when you want no infrastructure decisions at all.

questions.question: A research group must train a large language model from scratch on trillions of tokens and wants purpose-built AWS silicon that optimizes training price-performance. Which option should they choose?

options.text: Amazon EC2 instances powered by AWS Inferentia
options.rationale: Inferentia is optimized for low-cost, high-throughput inference rather than training.

options.text: Amazon EC2 instances powered by AWS Trainium
options.rationale: AWS Trainium is the AWS-designed accelerator for high-performance deep learning training, delivering strong price-performance for large model training on instances such as Trn1 and Trn2. AWS Inferentia is the sibling chip optimized for inference. Knowing which chip serves training and which serves inference is the point of this item.

options.text: AWS Graviton-based Amazon EC2 instances
options.rationale: Graviton processors are general-purpose CPUs for cost-efficient compute, not deep learning training accelerators.

options.text: Amazon EC2 instances with local NVMe storage only
options.rationale: Local storage affects data throughput but is not an accelerator for model training.

questions.question: A company self-hosts an open-weights text generation model on Amazon EC2 and wants to reduce the cost per inference while keeping throughput high. Which AWS purpose-built option targets this goal?

options.text: Amazon EC2 instances powered by AWS Trainium
options.rationale: Trainium is optimized for training, so it is a poor fit for reducing steady-state inference cost.

options.text: Amazon EC2 burstable T-family instances
options.rationale: Burstable general-purpose instances lack the accelerators needed for efficient model inference.

options.text: Amazon EC2 instances powered by AWS Inferentia
options.rationale: AWS Inferentia is the AWS-designed inference accelerator, available in Inf1 and Inf2 instances, built to lower cost per inference while sustaining high throughput and low latency. Trainium is its counterpart for training workloads. Both are accessed through the AWS Neuron SDK.

options.text: AWS Outposts racks in the company data center
options.rationale: Outposts extends AWS on premises for data residency needs and does not by itself reduce inference cost.

questions.question: An engineering team needs to compile and run a PyTorch model on AWS Trainium and AWS Inferentia based instances. Which software component should they use?

options.text: AWS Neuron SDK
options.rationale: The AWS Neuron SDK provides the compiler, runtime, and framework integrations that let PyTorch and other frameworks target Trainium and Inferentia accelerators. It is the bridge between standard ML code and AWS purpose-built silicon. Bedrock, by contrast, hides all of this behind managed APIs.

options.text: AWS CloudFormation
options.rationale: CloudFormation provisions infrastructure as code but does not compile models for accelerators.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Converse API
options.rationale: The Converse API is a Bedrock inference interface for managed models, not a compiler for custom silicon.

options.text: AWS Systems Manager Agent
options.rationale: The Systems Manager Agent supports instance management and patching, not model compilation.

questions.question: A team must run a custom generative model that requires specific CUDA libraries, kernel-level tuning, and full control of the operating system. Which AWS option is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock on-demand inference
options.rationale: Bedrock is fully managed and exposes no operating system or driver access.

options.text: Amazon EC2 GPU accelerated instances such as the P and G families
options.rationale: EC2 accelerated computing instances in the P and G families give full control of the operating system, drivers, and libraries, which is required when a workload depends on specific CUDA versions or low-level tuning. The tradeoff is that you own patching, scaling, and capacity management. Bedrock intentionally abstracts all of that away and therefore cannot expose kernel-level control.

options.text: Amazon Q Business
options.rationale: Amazon Q Business is a finished assistant product with no custom model hosting.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
options.rationale: Provisioned Throughput reserves managed Bedrock capacity and still provides no OS control.

questions.question: A startup uses Amazon Bedrock on-demand pricing for a text generation feature. Which factor MOST directly determines the monthly Bedrock bill?

options.text: The number of IAM users who can call the Bedrock API
options.rationale: IAM users are free and do not affect inference charges.

options.text: The amount of Amazon S3 storage in the same account
options.rationale: S3 storage is billed by S3 and is independent of Bedrock token pricing.

options.text: The number of AWS Regions enabled in the account
options.rationale: Enabling Regions incurs no charge by itself.

options.text: The number of input and output tokens processed by the chosen model
options.rationale: Bedrock on-demand pricing charges per input token and per output token at rates specific to each model, so token volume and model choice drive the bill. Reducing prompt length, capping output length, and selecting a smaller model are the primary cost levers. Storage and identity configuration are billed separately by other services.

questions.question: A customer-support automation currently uses one of the largest models on Amazon Bedrock for simple intent classification and template filling. Quality is far above what the task needs, and cost is a concern. Which change is the MOST cost-effective first step?

options.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the large model
options.rationale: Committing capacity for an oversized model locks in the inflated cost.

options.text: Move the workload to self-managed GPU instances on Amazon EC2
options.rationale: Self-managing GPUs adds operational burden and often costs more at this scale.

options.text: Switch the workload to a smaller, cheaper foundation model that still meets the accuracy bar
options.rationale: Model choice is one of the biggest generative AI cost levers: per-token rates differ dramatically between large frontier models and smaller models, and simple tasks rarely need the largest option. Validating a cheaper model against the accuracy requirement is a low-effort, high-impact optimization. Provisioned Throughput changes the purchasing model but not the underlying unit cost mismatch.

options.text: Increase the temperature parameter to reduce token usage
options.rationale: Temperature controls randomness of sampling and does not meaningfully reduce token counts.

questions.question: A generative AI feature has steady, predictable traffic around the clock at high volume. Finance modeling shows on-demand token charges now exceed the price of committed capacity for the same model. Which pricing decision is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Continue on-demand and enable prompt caching only
options.rationale: Prompt caching helps only for repeated prefixes and does not capture the committed-capacity discount for steady load.

options.text: Move all traffic to Amazon Bedrock batch inference
options.rationale: Batch inference is for asynchronous jobs and cannot serve real-time traffic.

options.text: Replicate the workload into a second Region to split the bill
options.rationale: Duplicating traffic across Regions changes nothing about total token cost.

options.text: Purchase Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput with a term commitment for the baseline load
options.rationale: When utilization is high and predictable, Provisioned Throughput with a commitment term typically becomes cheaper than paying per token, and it also guarantees capacity. The classic pattern is committed capacity for the baseline with on-demand absorbing spikes. Batch is not viable because the workload is interactive, and splitting Regions does not reduce total tokens.

questions.question: A hospital group is evaluating Amazon Bedrock and asks what happens to the prompts and completions it sends to third-party foundation models on the service. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Prompts are shared with model providers to improve their base models
options.rationale: Providers never receive customer content from Bedrock invocations.

options.text: Customer inputs and outputs are not shared with model providers and are not used to train the base models
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock does not share customer prompts or generated outputs with third-party model providers and does not use them to train the underlying foundation models. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest, and fine-tuning creates a private copy of the model for that customer. This data-privacy posture is a core advantage of using AWS managed generative AI.

options.text: AWS stores all prompts publicly for transparency
options.rationale: Prompts are private to the customer account; nothing is published.

options.text: Data privacy applies only if the company purchases Provisioned Throughput
options.rationale: Privacy protections apply to all Bedrock usage regardless of purchasing model.

questions.question: A startup founder must ship a generative AI chat feature in four weeks with two developers. The team is debating between building on Amazon Bedrock or pretraining its own model on rented GPU clusters. Which advantage of the managed approach is MOST relevant to this decision?

options.text: Managed services eliminate the need for prompt engineering
options.rationale: Prompt engineering is still needed regardless of who hosts the model.

options.text: Managed services guarantee the model will never produce incorrect output
options.rationale: No provider can guarantee generative output accuracy; hallucination remains a risk to manage.

options.text: Managed services provide immediate access to state-of-the-art models, dramatically reducing time to market
options.rationale: The decisive managed-service advantage here is speed to market: Bedrock exposes ready, state-of-the-art foundation models behind an API, so a small team can build the application layer immediately instead of spending months and large sums on pretraining. AWS also assumes the undifferentiated infrastructure, security, and scaling work. No service can promise correctness, and cost comparisons depend on scale.

options.text: Managed services are always cheaper per token than any self-hosted option
options.rationale: At very high sustained scale, self-hosting can sometimes be cheaper; the claim of always is false.

questions.question: A federal contractor must document that its generative AI workload runs on services covered by certifications such as SOC, ISO, and FedRAMP authorizations before it can proceed. How does using a managed service such as Amazon Bedrock help?

options.text: AWS maintains compliance certifications for the underlying service, which customers can reference through AWS Artifact
options.rationale: AWS operates Bedrock within its compliance programs, and customers can download attestations and certifications from AWS Artifact as evidence for their own audits. Under the shared responsibility model, AWS covers security of the cloud while the customer remains responsible for its data, configuration, and application behavior. Inheriting the platform certifications is a major advantage over certifying self-hosted infrastructure.

options.text: Compliance obligations transfer entirely to AWS, including the contractor's application-level responsibilities
options.rationale: Shared responsibility means the customer still owns application-level and data compliance.

options.text: Managed services are exempt from compliance audits
options.rationale: No AWS service is exempt from audits; AWS undergoes them and shares reports.

options.text: Bedrock automatically certifies the customer's application code
options.rationale: AWS certifies its services, not code the customer writes on top of them.

questions.question: A logistics company is comparing Amazon Bedrock with self-hosting foundation models on Amazon EC2. Which advantages does the managed Bedrock approach provide? (Select TWO.)

options.text: No servers, drivers, or model hosting infrastructure to manage
options.rationale: Bedrock's core advantages are serverless operation, which removes infrastructure management, and a single consistent API surface across multiple model providers so teams can switch or combine models easily. Neither hallucination nor the need for evaluation disappears. OS-level control is precisely what you give up in exchange for the managed experience.

options.text: Guaranteed elimination of hallucinated model output
options.rationale: No service can guarantee that generative output is always factually correct.

options.text: Access to multiple model providers through a consistent set of APIs
options.rationale: Bedrock's core advantages are serverless operation, which removes infrastructure management, and a single consistent API surface across multiple model providers so teams can switch or combine models easily. Neither hallucination nor the need for evaluation disappears. OS-level control is precisely what you give up in exchange for the managed experience.

options.text: Full control over the operating system and GPU driver versions
options.rationale: Low-level OS and driver control is an EC2 self-hosting benefit, not a Bedrock one.

options.text: Automatic removal of the need to evaluate model quality
options.rationale: Evaluating quality against your own data remains a customer responsibility.

questions.question: A media company wants to lower the cost of a high-volume Amazon Bedrock summarization workload without degrading output quality below its accuracy threshold. Which actions are likely to reduce cost? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Raise the top-k value on every request
options.rationale: Top-k changes sampling behavior and does not reduce billed tokens.

options.text: Trim redundant boilerplate from prompts and set a sensible maximum output token limit
options.rationale: Bedrock on-demand cost scales with input plus output tokens and with the model's per-token rate, so shortening prompts, capping response length, and routing simple traffic to a smaller model are direct savings. Sampling parameters and streaming affect output character and perceived latency, not billed token volume. Guardrails add a safety layer and their own charges rather than savings.

options.text: Add a second Guardrail policy to the workload
options.rationale: Adding a guardrail policy increases safety coverage and cost, not savings.

options.text: Route the highest-volume simple requests to a smaller model in the catalog
options.rationale: Bedrock on-demand cost scales with input plus output tokens and with the model's per-token rate, so shortening prompts, capping response length, and routing simple traffic to a smaller model are direct savings. Sampling parameters and streaming affect output character and perceived latency, not billed token volume. Guardrails add a safety layer and their own charges rather than savings.

options.text: Enable streaming responses with ConverseStream
options.rationale: Streaming improves perceived latency but bills the same tokens.

questions.question: An architect is deciding between Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI for a new project. Which requirements point toward SageMaker AI rather than Bedrock? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The team needs serverless access to third-party foundation models with no capacity planning
options.rationale: Serverless access to third-party foundation models is a Bedrock strength.

options.text: The team must train a custom model architecture from scratch on its own labeled dataset
options.rationale: SageMaker AI is the right choice when you need to build and train models yourself, with control over algorithms, containers, instance types, and distributed training. Bedrock is the right choice when you want managed access to existing foundation models with no infrastructure decisions. The dividing line on the exam is build-and-control versus consume-and-manage-nothing.

options.text: The team needs control over training instance types, distributed training configuration, and container images
options.rationale: SageMaker AI is the right choice when you need to build and train models yourself, with control over algorithms, containers, instance types, and distributed training. Bedrock is the right choice when you want managed access to existing foundation models with no infrastructure decisions. The dividing line on the exam is build-and-control versus consume-and-manage-nothing.

options.text: The team wants a visual, low-code workflow builder for chaining prompts
options.rationale: Visual low-code prompt chaining is Amazon Bedrock Flows.

options.text: The team wants to avoid managing any inference endpoints
options.rationale: Avoiding endpoint management points to Bedrock's serverless model.

questions.question: A financial firm is designing a secure Amazon Bedrock deployment and must satisfy its security team. Which statements about Bedrock security controls are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Bedrock requires all traffic to traverse the public internet
options.rationale: PrivateLink keeps traffic on the AWS network, so public internet transit is not required.

options.text: IAM identity-based policies can restrict which principals may invoke which foundation models
options.rationale: Bedrock integrates with IAM so you can scope permissions down to specific model invocations, and it supports AWS PrivateLink interface VPC endpoints so requests never leave the AWS network. API calls are also logged to AWS CloudTrail for auditing, and customer managed KMS keys can protect resources such as customized models. These controls are why regulated customers can adopt the service.

options.text: Bedrock API activity cannot be audited because the models are managed by third parties
options.rationale: Bedrock API calls are recorded in AWS CloudTrail, and model invocation logging is available.

options.text: Traffic from a VPC can reach Bedrock privately using AWS PrivateLink interface VPC endpoints
options.rationale: Bedrock integrates with IAM so you can scope permissions down to specific model invocations, and it supports AWS PrivateLink interface VPC endpoints so requests never leave the AWS network. API calls are also logged to AWS CloudTrail for auditing, and customer managed KMS keys can protect resources such as customized models. These controls are why regulated customers can adopt the service.

options.text: Customer-managed AWS KMS keys are unsupported for any Bedrock resource
options.rationale: Customer managed KMS keys are supported for encrypting Bedrock resources such as custom models.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical company is building an internal assistant and wants to know which AWS options require the LEAST application development. Which statements correctly describe the offerings? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Amazon Q Business is a ready-to-use assistant that connects to enterprise data sources with built-in connectors
options.rationale: Amazon Q Business is a packaged assistant with connectors and permission-aware retrieval, so it minimizes development work. Amazon Bedrock supplies building blocks, meaning the customer still writes the application around its APIs. JumpStart serves ML practitioners, and PartyRock is for learning and experimentation rather than production.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock provides finished end-user applications that need no development
options.rationale: Bedrock delivers APIs and capabilities, not finished end-user applications.

options.text: Building on Amazon Bedrock requires the company to develop the application layer around the model APIs
options.rationale: Amazon Q Business is a packaged assistant with connectors and permission-aware retrieval, so it minimizes development work. Amazon Bedrock supplies building blocks, meaning the customer still writes the application around its APIs. JumpStart serves ML practitioners, and PartyRock is for learning and experimentation rather than production.

options.text: SageMaker JumpStart is an end-user chat product for business teams
options.rationale: JumpStart is a model and solution hub for ML practitioners inside SageMaker AI.

options.text: PartyRock is the recommended platform for production enterprise assistants
options.rationale: PartyRock is a playground for learning, not a production enterprise platform.

questions.question: A public transit agency plans a generative AI trip-planning assistant. Which combinations correctly match an AWS capability to its role in the architecture? (Select TWO.)

options.text: AWS Trainium accelerators serve real-time inference at the lowest cost per request
options.rationale: Trainium is optimized for training; AWS Inferentia targets low-cost inference.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation blocks unsafe responses at inference time
options.rationale: Model Evaluation compares model quality offline and does not block responses at runtime.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides retrieval of the agency's service documents for grounded answers
options.rationale: Knowledge Bases supply managed retrieval so answers are grounded in the agency's own documents, and Guardrails enforce runtime safety policies on both input and output. Trainium targets training rather than cheapest inference, which is Inferentia's role. Model Evaluation is an offline quality process, and Model Monitor watches SageMaker endpoints for drift rather than redacting text.

options.text: SageMaker Model Monitor filters personally identifiable information from model output
options.rationale: Model Monitor detects drift and data quality issues on endpoints; Guardrails handle sensitive information filtering.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforces content and topic restrictions on prompts and responses
options.rationale: Knowledge Bases supply managed retrieval so answers are grounded in the agency's own documents, and Guardrails enforce runtime safety policies on both input and output. Trainium targets training rather than cheapest inference, which is Inferentia's role. Model Evaluation is an offline quality process, and Model Monitor watches SageMaker endpoints for drift rather than redacting text.

questions.question: A gaming studio needs sub-second responses for an in-game hint system and also runs a nightly job that rewrites thousands of quest descriptions. Which Amazon Bedrock choices best match these two workloads? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use batch inference for the nightly quest description rewrites to obtain a lower price per token
options.rationale: Batch inference fits the offline nightly rewrite job and is priced below real-time on-demand, while the latency-sensitive hint system needs synchronous invocation, optionally backed by Provisioned Throughput for guaranteed capacity. Matching the inference mode to latency tolerance is the core cost-and-performance decision. Custom Model Import does not remove usage charges, and Amazon Q Developer is a developer tool, not a player-facing runtime.

options.text: Use batch inference for the in-game hint system to reduce latency
options.rationale: Batch inference is asynchronous and increases latency, so it cannot serve in-game hints.

options.text: Use Provisioned Throughput or on-demand real-time invocation for the in-game hint system
options.rationale: Batch inference fits the offline nightly rewrite job and is priced below real-time on-demand, while the latency-sensitive hint system needs synchronous invocation, optionally backed by Provisioned Throughput for guaranteed capacity. Matching the inference mode to latency tolerance is the core cost-and-performance decision. Custom Model Import does not remove usage charges, and Amazon Q Developer is a developer tool, not a player-facing runtime.

options.text: Use Custom Model Import for both workloads to avoid token charges
options.rationale: Imported custom models still incur inference charges and add customization work.

options.text: Use Amazon Q Developer to serve the in-game hints to players
options.rationale: Amazon Q Developer assists engineers with coding, not end users in a game.

questions.question: A manufacturing firm wants to understand what Amazon Bedrock offers out of the box before designing its application. Which statements about Amazon Bedrock are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Bedrock requires customers to select and manage GPU instances for each model

options.rationale: Bedrock reuses existing foundation models; it does not pretrain a new model per customer.

options.rationale: Bedrock provides a catalog of foundation models from Amazon and partners such as Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Cohere, AI21 Labs, and Stability AI, and it supports customization through fine-tuning and continued pre-training, which produce a private copy of the model for your account. Capacity is managed by AWS, and access is available through the API, SDKs, and CLI in addition to the console.

options.text: Bedrock can be used only through the AWS Management Console

questions.question: A retail company is setting up an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base so its assistant can answer questions from product manuals. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: 1. Create the knowledge base and select an embeddings model and a vector store → 2. Run the ingestion job so documents are chunked, embedded, and written to the vector store → 3. options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Create the knowledge base and select an embeddings model and a vector store → 2. Store the product manuals in an Amazon S3 bucket as the data source → 3. Run the ingestion job so documents are chunked, embedded, and written to the vector store → 4. Query the knowledge base from the application and return grounded answers with citations
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

Run the ingestion job so documents are chunked, embedded, and written to the vector store → 4. Query the knowledge base from the application and return grounded answers with citations

questions.question: A media company maintains an internal HR policy library that is updated every week. The company wants an assistant built on Amazon Bedrock to answer employee questions using the latest policy text, with the least ongoing operational overhead. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Fine-tune a foundation model on the policy documents and rerun the fine-tuning job every week
options.rationale: Weekly fine-tuning jobs add recurring cost and effort, and the model still goes stale between runs.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to retrieve relevant policy passages at query time
options.rationale: Retrieval Augmented Generation leaves the model weights unchanged and injects freshly retrieved passages into the prompt, so keeping answers current is just a matter of re-syncing the knowledge base data source. Fine-tuning and continued pre-training bake knowledge into weights, so the information goes stale between training runs and each run costs time and money.

options.text: Run continued pre-training on the policy corpus each month
options.rationale: Continued pre-training needs large volumes of data and compute and is not a mechanism for keeping facts current.

options.text: Train a new foundation model from scratch on the company corpus
options.rationale: Training from scratch requires enormous data, compute, and expertise that this use case does not justify.

questions.question: A finance company uses a foundation model to generate regulatory report summaries and needs the output for a given prompt to be as repeatable and predictable as possible. Which inference parameter change best supports this requirement?

options.text: Increase the temperature value
options.rationale: Raising temperature increases randomness, which is the opposite of the requirement.

options.text: Increase the maximum output token limit
options.rationale: The maximum output token limit caps response length; it does not affect randomness.

options.text: Set the temperature to a value near 0
options.rationale: Temperature controls how much randomness is applied when sampling the next token. A value near 0 makes the model strongly favor the highest-probability tokens, producing more deterministic and consistent output, which suits compliance and reporting text. Higher temperature increases variety and creativity at the cost of repeatability.

options.text: Add several stop sequences to the request
options.rationale: Stop sequences control where generation ends, not how deterministic the wording is.

questions.question: A logistics startup wants a foundation model to write shipment status messages in the company's preferred tone and format. The team has a small budget and no ML engineers. Which customization approach should the team try FIRST?

options.text: Fine-tuning the model on 50,000 labeled message pairs
options.rationale: Fine-tuning requires a large curated dataset, training cost, and ML skills the team does not have.

options.text: Continued pre-training on the company's full document archive
options.rationale: Continued pre-training is one of the most expensive options and targets domain knowledge, not message tone.

options.text: Training a foundation model from scratch on shipping data
options.rationale: Training from scratch is the most expensive and complex option available and is not warranted here.

options.text: Prompt engineering that includes instructions and a few example messages
options.rationale: Customization approaches rise steeply in cost and complexity: prompt engineering, then RAG, then fine-tuning, then continued pre-training, then training from scratch. Prompt engineering needs no training infrastructure or labeled dataset and often solves tone and formatting requirements on its own, so it is the correct starting point.

questions.question: A healthcare analytics company is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation application and needs an AWS option that can store embeddings and run similarity search over them. Which options meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights
options.rationale: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries log data; it has no vector index or similarity search.

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector engine
options.rationale: A RAG application needs a vector store that indexes embeddings and supports nearest-neighbor search. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless offers a vector engine for this purpose, and Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL supports vector columns and similarity operators through the pgvector extension. Both are supported vector stores for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

options.text: AWS Glue Data Catalog
options.rationale: The Glue Data Catalog stores table and schema metadata, not embeddings.

options.text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension
options.rationale: A RAG application needs a vector store that indexes embeddings and supports nearest-neighbor search. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless offers a vector engine for this purpose, and Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL supports vector columns and similarity operators through the pgvector extension. Both are supported vector stores for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

options.text: Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
options.rationale: Glacier Deep Archive is low-cost archival object storage with retrieval delays and no search capability.

questions.question: A gaming company wants a customer support assistant that can look up a player's account balance through an internal REST API, issue a refund through a second API, and then summarize what it did. Which Amazon Bedrock capability is designed for this multistep, tool-invoking workflow?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
options.rationale: Guardrails filter harmful content and block denied topics; they do not orchestrate API calls.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation
options.rationale: Model Evaluation compares model quality on datasets; it does not run application workflows.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Agents break a user request into steps, decide which configured action group or API to call, pass the results back into the model, and continue until the task is complete. Knowledge Bases only retrieve text for grounding, while Guardrails and Model Evaluation address safety filtering and model comparison respectively.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
options.rationale: Knowledge Bases retrieve document passages for grounding but cannot invoke business APIs or take actions.

questions.question: A public sector agency must summarize 200-page environmental impact reports in a single model request without splitting the document, and the summary itself must run several pages long. Which two model selection criteria are MOST relevant to this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The size of the model's input context window
options.rationale: The context window determines how much source text a model can accept in one request, so it must be large enough to hold the full 200-page report. The maximum output token limit separately caps how long the generated summary can be, so both figures need to support this workload. Language coverage, output modality, and fine-tuning support do not address fitting or producing long text.

options.text: The number of languages the model supports
options.rationale: Multilingual support matters when handling multiple languages, which is not the stated constraint.

options.text: The model's maximum output token limit
options.rationale: The context window determines how much source text a model can accept in one request, so it must be large enough to hold the full 200-page report. The maximum output token limit separately caps how long the generated summary can be, so both figures need to support this workload. Language coverage, output modality, and fine-tuning support do not address fitting or producing long text.

options.text: The model's supported output modalities
options.rationale: Output modality matters when generating images or audio; this task produces text.

options.text: Whether the model supports fine-tuning
options.rationale: Fine-tuning support is unrelated to how much text fits in a request or how long a response can be.

questions.question: A retail company has a chatbot that answers product questions correctly but occasionally invents product specifications that do not exist. The company has an accurate product catalog in Amazon S3. Which approach BEST reduces these fabricated details?

options.text: Increase the temperature so the model explores more phrasings
options.rationale: Higher temperature increases randomness and typically makes fabrication more likely.

options.text: Ground responses by retrieving catalog data with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases and instructing the model to answer only from that data
options.rationale: Hallucination risk drops when the model is given authoritative source text and told to answer only from it. Retrieval from the product catalog grounds each response in enterprise data and lets the application cite sources. Changing sampling settings or output length does not supply the missing facts.

options.text: Increase the maximum output token limit so answers can be longer
options.rationale: A larger output limit allows longer answers but does nothing to make them factual.

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger number of supported languages
options.rationale: Multilingual capability is unrelated to factual grounding in company data.

questions.question: A manufacturing company needs a foundation model to consistently produce output in a specialized inspection report format, and thousands of labeled example reports are available. Prompt engineering with examples has produced inconsistent structure. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Retrieval Augmented Generation over the example reports
options.rationale: RAG supplies relevant context for factual grounding; it does not enforce a consistent output structure.

options.text: Continued pre-training on unlabeled manufacturing manuals
options.rationale: Continued pre-training builds domain vocabulary from unlabeled text rather than teaching a specific output format.

options.text: Fine-tuning the model on the labeled example reports
options.rationale: Fine-tuning adjusts model weights using labeled prompt and completion pairs, which is the right tool for teaching a consistent style, structure, or task behavior that prompting cannot reliably enforce. RAG adds facts at query time but does not reshape output format, and continued pre-training targets broad domain knowledge from unlabeled text.

options.text: Increasing top-k so the model considers more candidate tokens
options.rationale: Raising top-k widens token sampling and increases variability, worsening consistency.

questions.question: A bank is setting up a Retrieval Augmented Generation workflow on Amazon Bedrock. Place the data ingestion and query steps in the correct order.

options.text: 1. Retrieve the most similar chunks for a user question and pass them to the foundation model in the prompt → 2. Store the resulting vectors and metadata in a vector index → 3. Convert each chunk into a vector by calling an embedding model → 4. Split the source documents into chunks
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.text: 1. Split the source documents into chunks → 2. Convert each chunk into a vector by calling an embedding model → 3. Store the resulting vectors and metadata in a vector index → 4. Retrieve the most similar chunks for a user question and pass them to the foundation model in the prompt
options.rationale: RAG ingestion starts by chunking source documents so each piece fits the embedding model and represents a coherent idea. Each chunk is then embedded into a vector, and the vectors are written to a vector index with metadata. At query time the user question is embedded, the nearest chunks are retrieved, and they are added to the prompt so the model answers from grounded context.

options.text: 1. Convert each chunk into a vector by calling an embedding model → 2. Store the resulting vectors and metadata in a vector index → 3. Retrieve the most similar chunks for a user question and pass them to the foundation model in the prompt → 4. Split the source documents into chunks
options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

questions.question: A marketing team wants a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock to generate campaign images from text descriptions. Which model selection criterion determines whether a candidate model can meet this requirement?

options.text: The model's fine-tuning support
options.rationale: Fine-tuning support affects customization options, not whether the model can output images.

options.text: The model's supported input and output modalities
options.rationale: Modality describes the types of data a model accepts and produces, such as text, image, audio, or video. Only a model whose output modality includes images can generate images from text prompts, so modality is a hard filter applied before considering cost or customization support.

options.text: The model's maximum temperature setting
options.rationale: Temperature is a sampling control available on text generation requests, not a capability filter.

options.text: The model's token pricing tier
options.rationale: Pricing influences the final choice but cannot make a text-only model produce images.

questions.question: A travel company runs a voice ordering assistant where users expect a spoken reply within about one second. Two Amazon Bedrock models produce acceptable quality, but one is much larger and slower. Which selection decision BEST fits the requirement?

options.text: Choose the larger model and raise the maximum output token limit
options.rationale: A larger model plus longer outputs increases latency, moving away from the one-second target.

options.text: Choose the larger model and increase top-p to speed up sampling
options.rationale: Top-p changes how tokens are sampled and has no effect on inference speed.

options.text: Choose the larger model and add more few-shot examples to the prompt
options.rationale: Additional few-shot examples enlarge the prompt and add processing time.

options.text: Choose the smaller, faster model to reduce inference latency
options.rationale: When quality is comparable, a smaller model generally delivers lower latency and lower cost per request, which matters for interactive real-time experiences. Larger prompts and longer outputs increase response time, and top-p is a sampling control that does not affect generation speed.

questions.question: An insurance company is deciding between Retrieval Augmented Generation and fine-tuning for a claims assistant. Which situations favor RAG over fine-tuning? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The underlying policy documents change several times per week
options.rationale: RAG excels when the knowledge changes frequently and when traceability matters, because content lives in a data store that can be updated independently and retrieved passages can be surfaced as citations. Fine-tuning is the better fit for durable behavior changes such as style or task format, and it can shrink prompts by moving instructions into the weights.

options.text: The company needs the model to permanently adopt a new writing style
options.rationale: Permanent style adoption is a behavior change, which fine-tuning handles better than retrieval.

options.text: Responses must cite the specific source document used for each answer
options.rationale: RAG excels when the knowledge changes frequently and when traceability matters, because content lives in a data store that can be updated independently and retrieved passages can be surfaced as citations. Fine-tuning is the better fit for durable behavior changes such as style or task format, and it can shrink prompts by moving instructions into the weights.

options.text: The company wants to shorten prompts to reduce per-request token cost
options.rationale: Fine-tuning is what reduces prompt length; RAG adds retrieved context and increases token usage.

options.text: The company wants the model to learn a new low-resource language
options.rationale: Teaching a new language requires extensive training such as continued pre-training, not retrieval.

questions.question: A media company converts its article archive into numerical representations so that semantically similar articles cluster together for retrieval. What are these numerical representations called?

options.text: Tokens
options.rationale: Tokens are the sub-word units a model reads and generates, not semantic vectors used for similarity search.

options.text: Hyperparameters
options.rationale: Hyperparameters are training configuration values such as learning rate or epochs.

options.text: Model weights
options.rationale: Model weights are the learned parameters inside the model itself, not per-document representations.

options.text: Embeddings
options.rationale: An embedding is a dense vector that encodes the meaning of a piece of text, image, or other input, so that items with similar meaning sit close together in vector space. Retrieval systems store embeddings in a vector index and compare them by distance or cosine similarity.

questions.question: A logistics company sees that its foundation model responses are sometimes cut off in the middle of a sentence. Which change is MOST likely to resolve the issue?

options.text: Lower the temperature value
options.rationale: Lower temperature makes wording more predictable but does not extend the allowed response length.

options.text: Reduce top-k to a smaller number
options.rationale: A smaller top-k narrows candidate tokens and does not change the length limit.

options.text: Increase the maximum number of output tokens allowed in the response
options.rationale: Truncation mid-sentence usually means generation hit the configured output token limit. Raising that limit, within the model's supported range, lets the response finish. Temperature and top-k change which tokens are selected, not how many tokens the model is allowed to produce.

options.text: Switch to a model with more supported languages
options.rationale: Language coverage is unrelated to response truncation.

questions.question: A global retailer needs one foundation model to handle customer chat in English, Japanese, Portuguese, and Arabic with consistent quality. Which model selection criterion should drive the choice?

options.text: Vector store compatibility
options.rationale: Vector store compatibility matters for retrieval architecture, not language quality.

options.text: Multilingual support across the required languages
options.rationale: Foundation models differ substantially in how well they handle languages other than English, so multilingual capability is the criterion that determines whether a single model can serve all four markets. If no single model performs well enough, the alternative is routing per language, but the evaluation criterion is still language coverage.

options.text: Support for image input
options.rationale: Image input is irrelevant to a text chat requirement.

options.text: Availability of a batch inference option
options.rationale: Batch inference suits offline bulk jobs, not interactive multilingual chat quality.

questions.question: A company must rank four customization approaches from lowest to highest cost and complexity before choosing one. Which ordering is correct?

options.text: Fine-tuning, prompt engineering, RAG, continued pre-training
options.rationale: This places fine-tuning below prompt engineering, which reverses the actual cost relationship.

options.text: RAG, prompt engineering, continued pre-training, fine-tuning
options.rationale: This places RAG below prompt engineering and misorders the two training approaches.

options.text: Prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning, continued pre-training
options.rationale: Cost and complexity increase in this order: prompt engineering, which requires only request changes; RAG, which adds a retrieval pipeline and vector store; fine-tuning, which requires labeled data and a training job; and continued pre-training, which requires very large unlabeled corpora and substantial compute. Training a model from scratch sits beyond all four.

options.text: Continued pre-training, fine-tuning, RAG, prompt engineering
options.rationale: This lists the approaches from most expensive to least expensive rather than the reverse.

questions.question: A hospital network wants to generate 90,000 discharge summary drafts overnight from records already stored in Amazon S3, with no interactive latency requirement and minimal cost. Which two statements about Amazon Bedrock batch inference are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Batch inference processes large sets of prompts asynchronously and is priced lower than on-demand per-request inference
options.rationale: Batch inference submits large sets of prompts, reading inputs from and writing outputs to Amazon S3, and is billed at a lower rate than on-demand per-request calls because it runs asynchronously with no latency guarantee. This fits an overnight, non-interactive workload where minimizing cost matters more than response time.

options.text: Batch inference reads input records from Amazon S3 and writes results back to Amazon S3
options.rationale: Batch inference submits large sets of prompts, reading inputs from and writing outputs to Amazon S3, and is billed at a lower rate than on-demand per-request calls because it runs asynchronously with no latency guarantee. This fits an overnight, non-interactive workload where minimizing cost matters more than response time.

options.text: Batch inference reserves dedicated model capacity that continues after the job completes
options.rationale: Reserved capacity that persists is a feature of Provisioned Throughput, not batch inference.

options.text: An application must run a batch job before it is allowed to call a model on demand
options.rationale: Batch inference and on-demand inference are independent options; neither is a prerequisite for the other.

options.text: Batch inference supports sub-second response times suitable for live chat
options.rationale: Batch jobs complete over minutes to hours and cannot serve live, interactive chat traffic.

questions.question: A gaming company wants a foundation model to write varied item descriptions but must avoid rare, off-topic word choices. The team wants the model to sample only from the smallest set of most probable tokens whose cumulative probability reaches a threshold. Which inference parameter provides this behavior?

options.text: Top-p
options.rationale: Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest set of candidate tokens whose probabilities sum to the configured threshold, so the candidate pool shrinks when the model is confident and widens when it is not. Top-k instead keeps a fixed count of candidates regardless of how the probabilities are distributed.

options.text: Top-k
options.rationale: Top-k caps the candidate list at a fixed number of tokens rather than a cumulative probability mass.

options.text: Maximum output tokens
options.rationale: Maximum output tokens limits response length, not token selection.

options.text: Stop sequences
options.rationale: Stop sequences end generation at specified strings and do not influence candidate selection.

questions.question: A public utility is designing a RAG assistant over 4 million maintenance records and expects thousands of concurrent employee queries at peak. Which two considerations are MOST important when selecting the vector store? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Support for image generation
options.rationale: Image generation is unrelated to a vector store's role in retrieval.

options.text: Query latency and scalability of the vector index at the required scale
options.rationale: In a RAG application, every user query triggers a similarity search before the model is called, so the vector store contributes directly to end-to-end latency and must scale to the document volume and query concurrency the utility expects, both now and as records grow. Image generation, stop sequences, and automatic embedding fine-tuning are unrelated to how a vector store performs retrieval.

options.text: The number of stop sequences the store can hold
options.rationale: Stop sequences are inference request settings, not a vector store feature.

options.text: The ability to index and search millions of embeddings without a redesign
options.rationale: In a RAG application, every user query triggers a similarity search before the model is called, so the vector store contributes directly to end-to-end latency and must scale to the document volume and query concurrency the utility expects, both now and as records grow. Image generation, stop sequences, and automatic embedding fine-tuning are unrelated to how a vector store performs retrieval.

options.text: Whether the store can fine-tune the embedding model automatically
options.rationale: Vector stores index embeddings; they do not train or fine-tune embedding models.

questions.question: A university wants an internal assistant that answers student questions using its own course catalog rather than general internet knowledge. Which capability best describes what the university needs?

options.text: Grounding model responses in enterprise data
options.rationale: Grounding means supplying the model with authoritative organizational content at inference time so answers reflect that data instead of the model's general pre-training knowledge. This is exactly what a retrieval-based design over the course catalog provides.

options.text: Reducing the model's parameter count
options.rationale: Reducing parameters affects speed and cost, not which data the answers come from.

options.text: Increasing the model's temperature
options.rationale: Higher temperature adds randomness and does not introduce institutional data.

options.text: Converting the model to a smaller quantized format
options.rationale: Quantization optimizes inference efficiency and has no effect on data grounding.

questions.question: An airline wants an assistant that can check seat availability, rebook a passenger, and email a confirmation in response to one natural language request. The team wants to minimize custom orchestration code. Which design should the team choose?

options.text: A single large prompt that describes all three tasks and asks the model to output the final email text
options.rationale: A prompt can draft text but cannot query availability or perform a booking action.

options.text: A fine-tuned model trained on past rebooking transcripts
options.rationale: Fine-tuning improves how the model writes about rebooking; it cannot execute the rebooking.

options.text: An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base built from the airline's fare rules
options.rationale: A knowledge base retrieves fare rule text and cannot invoke booking or email APIs.

options.text: An Amazon Bedrock agent with action groups mapped to the booking and notification APIs
options.rationale: Agents provide the reasoning loop and action invocation that multistep tasks require: the agent plans the steps, calls each configured API, and uses the returned data to continue. A prompt alone cannot change system state, fine-tuning only alters generated text, and a knowledge base only supplies reference passages.

questions.question: A financial services firm is reviewing its Amazon Bedrock spend for a text summarization feature. Which actions will reduce inference cost? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Trim redundant boilerplate from prompts to lower input token counts
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock on-demand pricing is driven by input and output tokens and by the model chosen, so cutting unnecessary prompt content and using the smallest model that meets quality requirements both lower cost directly. Larger output limits and extra examples increase token counts, and temperature has no bearing on price.

options.text: Raise the maximum output token limit for every request
options.rationale: Allowing longer outputs tends to increase output tokens and therefore cost.

options.text: Select a smaller model that still meets the quality bar for summarization
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock on-demand pricing is driven by input and output tokens and by the model chosen, so cutting unnecessary prompt content and using the smallest model that meets quality requirements both lower cost directly. Larger output limits and extra examples increase token counts, and temperature has no bearing on price.

options.text: Increase temperature to shorten responses
options.rationale: Temperature affects randomness, not response length or price.

options.text: Add five more few-shot examples to every prompt
options.rationale: More few-shot examples add input tokens to every request, raising cost.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical research group needs a foundation model that understands highly specialized biochemistry vocabulary that appears rarely in general web text. options.text: Few-shot prompting with three example answers

options.text: Continued pre-training on the unlabeled research corpus
options.rationale: Continued pre-training extends a base model's knowledge using large volumes of unlabeled domain text, which is what this group has. Supervised fine-tuning requires labeled input and output pairs, and training from scratch would cost far more than adapting an existing model.

options.text: Supervised fine-tuning on the unlabeled documents
options.rationale: Supervised fine-tuning requires labeled prompt and completion pairs, which the group does not have.

options.text: Training a foundation model from scratch
options.rationale: Training from scratch demands vastly more data, compute, and expertise than adapting an existing model.

questions.question: A news organization built a RAG assistant, but reviewers report that answers frequently miss details that clearly exist in the source articles. The retrieval step returns passages that end mid-topic. Which change should the team evaluate FIRST?

options.text: Lower the temperature to zero
options.rationale: Temperature affects wording variability, not what content retrieval returns.

options.text: Switch the response to a different output language
options.rationale: Output language has no effect on retrieval quality.

options.text: Adjust the document chunking strategy, including chunk size and overlap
options.rationale: In RAG, chunking determines what a single retrievable unit contains. Chunks that are too small or that split across a topic boundary cause incomplete context to reach the model. Tuning chunk size and adding overlap keeps related sentences together and usually improves answer completeness before any model change is needed.

options.text: Reduce the maximum output token limit
options.rationale: A smaller output limit would truncate answers further rather than restore missing detail.

questions.question: A retail analytics team needs guaranteed inference capacity and consistent throughput for a customer-facing assistant that receives steady high traffic all day. Which Amazon Bedrock option addresses this requirement?

options.text: Batch inference jobs scheduled hourly

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation
options.rationale: Model Evaluation measures response quality; it does not reserve capacity.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
options.rationale: Guardrails filter content; they have no role in capacity planning.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput for the selected model
options.rationale: Provisioned Throughput reserves model capacity measured in model units, giving predictable throughput and consistent performance for sustained production traffic. Batch inference is asynchronous and unsuitable for live chat, while Model Evaluation and Guardrails address quality comparison and content safety.

questions.question: A telecommunications company wants to compare three Amazon Bedrock foundation models on its own summarization prompts before selecting one for production. Which capability supports this comparison with the least custom tooling?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation runs automatic or human evaluation jobs against selected models using built-in or custom prompt datasets and reports comparable metrics, which is exactly what model selection requires. The other services address feature management, workflow orchestration, and data labeling.

options.text: SageMaker Feature Store
options.rationale: Feature Store stores and serves ML features for training and inference, not model comparisons.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Flows
options.rationale: Flows chains prompts and components into a workflow; it does not score model quality.

options.text: SageMaker Ground Truth

questions.question: A construction firm must keep its assistant's answers current with contract amendments that arrive daily, and auditors require the exact source paragraph for each answer. Which design meets both requirements?

options.text: Fine-tune a model nightly on the amended contracts
options.rationale: Nightly fine-tuning is expensive and provides no source attribution for auditors.

options.text: Use a knowledge base with citations returned alongside each generated answer
options.rationale: A retrieval design keeps content in a data source that syncs on a schedule and returns the retrieved passages, which can be surfaced as citations for audit. Training approaches cannot attribute an answer to a specific source paragraph, and pasting the entire archive into every prompt is costly and hits context limits.

options.text: Increase the context window and paste all contracts into every prompt
options.rationale: Sending the full archive on every request wastes tokens and will exceed practical context limits.

options.text: Use continued pre-training weekly on the contract archive
options.rationale: Weekly continued pre-training leaves answers stale and cannot cite specific paragraphs.

questions.question: A logistics platform reports that end-to-end response time for its RAG assistant has grown to eight seconds. Investigation shows the retrieval step is fast, but the prompt now includes 20 retrieved passages and requests very long answers. Which change is MOST likely to reduce latency?

options.text: Return fewer, higher-relevance passages and cap the output length
options.rationale: Inference latency scales with the number of tokens processed in the prompt and generated in the response. Since retrieval is already fast, trimming the retrieved context to the most relevant passages and limiting output length directly cuts token processing time. Sampling settings do not change generation speed.

options.text: Move the vector index to a larger instance family
options.rationale: Scaling the vector store will not help because retrieval is not the bottleneck.

options.text: Raise the temperature to speed up token selection
options.rationale: Temperature affects randomness only and has no impact on speed.

options.text: Increase the number of retrieved passages to improve recall
options.rationale: More passages add input tokens and increase latency further.

options.rationale: That is not the correct order for these steps.

questions.question: A bank plans to build an internal assistant that answers employee questions from documents stored in Amazon S3 and SharePoint, with built-in connectors and access controls, and minimal development work. Which service should the bank use?

options.text: Amazon Q Business
options.rationale: Amazon Q Business is a managed generative AI assistant that connects to enterprise data sources, respects existing user permissions, and answers questions with citations, so it requires far less engineering than assembling a custom retrieval application. options.text: Amazon Polly

options.text: Amazon Textract
options.rationale: Textract extracts text and structure from documents but does not provide conversational answers.

questions.question: A company must choose between a 7-billion-parameter model and a much larger model for classifying support tickets into 12 categories. Accuracy tests show both meet the target. Which consideration MOST supports choosing the smaller model?

options.text: The smaller model supports more input modalities
options.rationale: Modality support depends on the specific model, not on having fewer parameters.

options.text: The smaller model generally offers lower cost per token and faster responses
options.rationale: Model size correlates with inference cost and latency, so when a smaller model already meets the accuracy bar, it is the better economic and performance choice. Size does not by itself determine modality support, factual accuracy, or the need for good prompts.

options.text: The smaller model always produces more factual answers
options.rationale: Smaller models are not inherently more factual; larger models often perform better on complex reasoning.

options.text: The smaller model removes the need for prompt engineering
options.rationale: Prompt engineering remains necessary regardless of model size.

questions.question: A manufacturer is designing an Amazon Bedrock agent that troubleshoots equipment faults across several backend systems. Which statements about agents are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: An agent can break a request into multiple steps and decide which action to invoke at each step
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Agents use a foundation model to plan a sequence of steps, invoke action groups backed by APIs or AWS Lambda functions, and can also query an associated knowledge base for grounding within the same conversation. Agents rely on a model rather than replacing it, provide no factual guarantee, and require no fine-tuning to call actions.

options.text: An agent replaces the need for a foundation model in the application
options.rationale: Agents orchestrate a foundation model; the model is still what generates the reasoning and text.

options.text: An agent can combine API actions with retrieval from a knowledge base in the same session
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Agents use a foundation model to plan a sequence of steps, invoke action groups backed by APIs or AWS Lambda functions, and can also query an associated knowledge base for grounding within the same conversation. Agents rely on a model rather than replacing it, provide no factual guarantee, and require no fine-tuning to call actions.

options.text: An agent must be fine-tuned before it can call any API

options.text: Amazon Neptune property graphs

questions.question: A retailer's legal team requires that any third-party foundation model's license permit the intended commercial use of generated outputs, and its infrastructure team wants the flexibility to run the model through a fully managed API today with the option to self-host later if costs change. options.text: Whether the model's license terms permit the intended commercial use of its outputs

Default throughput quotas can usually be raised through support requests, stop sequence limits are a minor inference detail, and a model's release date does not by itself reveal licensing or deployment options.

options.text: The model's default maximum tokens per minute quota
options.rationale: Default quota limits can typically be raised through support requests and do not address licensing or deployment flexibility.

options.text: Whether the model is available through both a managed API and self-managed deployment options
options.rationale: License terms determine whether the retailer is legally permitted to use the model's outputs commercially, and deployment flexibility determines whether the model can move from a managed API to self-managed infrastructure without switching model families. Default throughput quotas can usually be raised through support requests, stop sequence limits are a minor inference detail, and a model's release date does not by itself reveal licensing or deployment options.

options.text: The number of stop sequences the model supports per request
options.rationale: Stop sequence support is a minor inference feature unrelated to licensing or where the model can run.

options.text: Whether the model was first released before or after a specific calendar year
options.rationale: Release date alone does not indicate licensing terms or which deployment options exist.

questions.question: A mortgage lender fine-tuned a model on 6,000 historical underwriting notes. The custom model performs well on wording style but still cites outdated interest rate tables. Which additional design change addresses the outdated figures?

options.text: Increase the number of fine-tuning epochs
options.rationale: More epochs reinforce the same outdated training data and risk overfitting.

options.text: Add a retrieval step that supplies the current rate tables in the prompt
options.rationale: Fine-tuning teaches style and task behavior but freezes whatever facts were in the training data. Volatile reference data belongs in a retrieval layer so each request receives the current values. Fine-tuning and RAG are complementary, and sampling parameters cannot correct stale facts.

options.text: Lower the temperature to zero for all requests
options.rationale: A temperature of zero makes the model repeat the stale figures more consistently.

options.text: Raise top-k so more candidate tokens are considered
options.rationale: Top-k changes token sampling and has no effect on factual currency.
